10039-the-works-of-aphra-behn-volume-iii:
Montague Summers edited this third volume of Aphra Behn's works in 1915, gathering five of her Restoration plays. Behn, the first Englishwoman to earn her living by writing, wrote comedies of wit, money, and desire for the London stage.

The volume holds The Town-Fop, or Sir Timothy Tawdrey, and The False Count. It adds The Lucky Chance, or An Alderman's Bargain, The Forc'd Marriage, or The Jealous Bridegroom, and The Emperor of the Moon, with notes. Readers meet a bold, funny playwright whose heroines scheme as cleverly as any hero.
10513-on-the-seashore-cassell-s-eyes-and:
R. Cadwallader Smith wrote this seventh book of Cassell's Eyes and No Eyes series, on the seashore, with color plates and many black-and-white pictures. The series teaches children to look closely at nature, rather than to pass it by with no eyes. Each lesson names a shore creature or plant in plain words.

Lessons treat five-fingered Jack, a stroll by the sea, shore birds, crabs, shrimps, prawns, barnacles, shore plants, flower-like animals, seaweeds, jelly-fish, and shells with their builders. Gulls and redshanks appear in color. Readers get a charming, old-style nature primer for the beach.
10617-within-the-deep-cassell-s-eyes-and:
R. Cadwallader Smith wrote Within the Deep as the eighth book of Cassell's "Eyes and No Eyes" series, which taught children to observe nature. Eight colored plates and many black-and-white pictures show the herring fleet, sea-elephants, coral reefs, and whaling ships. The lessons are short and plain, made for young readers.

Chapters cover fish for breakfast, flat fish, seals, strange sea nurseries, the whale, tigers of the sea, rock-pools, and the garden of the sea. Smith begins with the herring, which fed millions and built whole towns. Children get a vivid first natural history of ocean life, and adults get a charming sample of Edwardian science teaching.
10693-a-political-diary-1828-1830-volume:
Edward Law, Lord Ellenborough, kept a political diary while serving in the Duke of Wellington's government, and this second volume, edited by Lord Colchester and published in 1881, covers 1828 to 1830. Its entries record cabinet dinners, Commons business, petitions, and the daily grind of governing. One April 1829 entry notes Wellington writing to the King about galleries for visitors.

The diary gives an insider's view of high politics in the years of Catholic emancipation and reform agitation. Ellenborough writes briefly and frankly, noting who said what and what was decided. Historians value it for detail no formal history preserves, and general readers get politics as it felt day by day.
10828-roman-history-books-i-iii:
Livy, or Titus Livius, wrote a Roman History that stands among the greatest works of Latin prose. This 1904 volume holds Books I to III in translations by Freese, Church, and Brodribb. An introduction by Duffield Osborne laments the lost books of Livy, which survived nearly whole into the fifth century and perhaps the fifteenth. The tale that Pope Gregory I ordered their destruction is, Osborne says, unproven.

The surviving early books tell Rome from its founding through kings and early republic. Livy's moral narrative, full of heroes and warnings, shaped how later ages saw Rome. Readers get the opening of a masterpiece, in clear Victorian translation.
1103-king-richard-iii:
Richard, Duke of Gloucester, crooked in body and boundless in will, murders his way to the crown of England in William Shakespeare's history play. He charms, lies, and kills: brothers, nephews, wives, and friends fall as he clears his road, while ghosts and curses gather behind him.

Richard's wit makes him a magnetic villain, and his soliloquies let the audience share his plots. At Bosworth Field his luck runs out, and Henry Tudor takes the crown. The play made "my kingdom for a horse" famous, and it remains the great stage portrait of a tyrant's rise and fall.
1111-king-richard-ii:
King Richard II of England, graceful, vain, and sure of God's favor, banishes his cousin Bolingbroke and seizes his lands, then loses his crown to him. William Shakespeare's history play tracks Richard's fall from anointed king to a prisoner who finds, too late, the poet in himself.

The verse is rich and ceremonial, full of gardens, mirrors, and crowned heads as symbols of rule. Bolingbroke's cold competence beats Richard's fine words. The play asks what makes a king: blood, law, or power. It remains a favorite of actors for its great central role.
1136-king-henry-viii:
William Shakespeare's last history play follows the reign of Henry VIII. It shows the fall of Cardinal Wolsey, the king's divorce from Katharine of Aragon, and his marriage to Anne Boleyn, mother of the future Elizabeth. Court plots, trials, and pageants crowd the stage.

Wolsey's fall and Katharine's dignity give the play its emotional weight, while the birth of Elizabeth closes it in prophecy and praise. Scholars think John Fletcher shared in the writing. The play offers a rich, ceremonial view of Tudor power, and it still draws crowds for its pageantry.
1503-king-richard-iii:
Shakespeare's Richard III follows the crookbacked Duke of Gloucester as he murders, woos, and lies his way to the crown of England. From a London street to the Tower, Richard clears his brother Clarence, his nephews the princes, and every rival, all while sharing his plans with the audience in dazzling asides.

Ghosts of his victims haunt him before Bosworth Field, where Richmond defeats him and ends the Wars of the Roses. Richard's wit makes him horrifying and magnetic at once. The play is Shakespeare's first great villain study, and a masterpiece of political theatre.
1512-king-richard-ii:
Shakespeare's history of Richard II opens with a quarrel between Bolingbroke and Mowbray, settled by banishment rather than combat. When Richard seizes Bolingbroke's inheritance, the exile returns with an army, and the king, a poet in a crown, loses his throne piece by piece in scenes of great lyric power.

The deposition scene, in which Richard hands over his crown and breaks the mirror of his kingship, is among Shakespeare's finest. Bolingbroke takes the crown as Henry IV, and Richard dies a prisoner. The play is a meditation on kingship, language, and the fall of a ruler who ruled by words.
1541-king-henry-viii:
Shakespeare's Henry VIII follows the king's divorce from Katherine of Aragon, his marriage to Anne Boleyn, and the fall of Cardinal Wolsey, from a London ante-chamber to Blackfriars and Westminster. Katherine's dignity, Wolsey's pride, and Cranmer's rise give the chronicle its human centres.

The play ends with the christening of the infant Elizabeth and a prophecy of her golden reign. Its pageantry is rich and its politics are courtly. Henry VIII is Shakespeare's last history, a stately pageant of power, marriage, and a kingdom changing its faith. Its pageantry and court scenes remain splendid theatre.
1565-the-last-days-of-pompeii:
Edward Bulwer-Lytton's Last Days of Pompeii opens with two gentlemen of Pompeii, Glaucus and Clodius, supping and gossiping in a city unaware of its doom. Around them gather a blind flower girl, a priest of Isis, a gladiator, and lovers whose fates converge as Vesuvius stirs.

The novel builds from daily life, baths, and theatres to the eruption itself, when ash buries streets and the survivors flee by sea. Lytton's romance is grand and sentimental. It remains the most famous Pompeii novel, and a vivid, if old-fashioned, picture of a Roman city on its last day.
1677-alcibiades-ii:
This dialogue was written by an imitator of Plato in the second or third generation after him. Translated by Benjamin Jowett, it takes the form of a talk between Socrates and the young Alcibiades about prayer. Alcibiades is about to pray for success, and Socrates stops him to ask whether he knows what he is really asking for.

The argument is that men often pray for wealth, power, or command, and then find those gifts bring ruin. Socrates urges Alcibiades to pray only for what is good, and to admit how little he knows. The dialogue is not Plato's own, but it shows his school at work, turning a familiar habit into a question about wisdom.
1770-king-edward-iii:
The Reign of King Edward the Third, attributed in part to William Shakespeare, dramatizes the early Hundred Years' War: Edward's claim to France, the Black Prince's campaigns, and the siege of Calais. The cast runs from Edward and his queen Philippa to John of France, the Countess of Salisbury, and six citizens of Calais who offer their lives for their town.

The play's authorship has long been debated, and its verse moves between high rhetoric and plain speech. Its best-known scenes — Edward's wooing of the Countess, and the citizens' surrender — give the play its lasting interest. It is now read as a bridge between Shakespeare's histories and the work of his fellows.
1879-royalty-restored-or-london-under-ch:
J. Fitzgerald Molloy tells the story of London under Charles II, when royalty was restored after the Commonwealth and the city relearned pleasure. The book follows the court, the theatres, and the town, with countesses and ladies dressing a bride in English fashion, in a habit they thought would please the king.

Molloy writes history as pageant, with anecdotes of courtiers, actresses, and politicians crowding the chapters. The volume works as a readable introduction to Restoration London. Its charm lies in its detail: a city shaking off Puritan rule and dressing itself, quite literally, for a new reign.
19717-the-bostonians-vol-i-of-ii:
Henry James published The Bostonians in 1886, and it remains among his sharpest American novels. Volume one of two opens with a Southern visitor arriving in Boston. A lady in the scene teases him about being a Southerner. Olive Chancellor, the hostess, has sent word hoping he will stay to dinner. The visitor is her cousin, Basil Ransom, a Mississippian lawyer in New York.

James pits Ransom against Olive for the future of a young speaker, Verena Tarrant. Reform-era Boston, with its causes and drawing rooms, fills the stage. The novel's real fight is over ideas, charm, and control. James tells it in dense, ironic prose. Volume one sets the triangle that volume two will tighten.
20102-the-international-monthly-magazine:
The International Monthly Magazine, volume five, number two, gathers essays and reviews for its readers. One piece weighs the fame of a famed general of the Peninsula War. It grants him rare skill in many fields of command. Yet it denies him the first rank among great generals of history.

That fame, it argues, rests much on Napier's glowing history of the war. Napier wrote with skill but also with clear bias, the essay says. Monthly magazines then served as courts for such debates on fame. Readers get a sharp sample of 1850s literary and military argument.
20300-henry-viii:
Henry VIII, in this biography, first appeared in June 1902 with many pictures. A new edition came in May 1905 from Longmans, Green and Company. It was reprinted in January 1913 and again in October 1919. Its author also wrote lives of Cranmer and of Protector Somerset.

Henry remains one of England's most debated and dramatic kings. Six wives, a broken church, and vast power mark his reign. A life of Henry must weigh charm against cruelty at each turn. Readers get a scholarly yet readable portrait from a seasoned Tudor historian. Later lives have judged him more harshly, but few match this one's steady learning.
20947-memoirs-of-the-jacobites-of-1715-a:
Royal favour, high missions, and rich marriages built one family's power in volume two. Memoirs of the Jacobites traces such houses across the risings of 1715 and 1745. Intermarriage with Scotland's richest, noblest lines swelled their sway by degrees.

More lives of Stuart loyalists fill this second volume of Thomson's set. Exile, plots, scaffolds, and stubborn hope mark their varied ends. Family papers give the tales their warmth and their proof. Together the volumes keep a whole lost cause in view, through the men and women who paid its price in full.
20948-memoirs-of-the-jacobites-of-1715-a:
Letters never before in print grace the life of the Earl of Kilmarnock in volume three. Family helpers aided the Derwentwater life with zeal and exact knowledge. Memoirs of the Jacobites closes its set with Charles Radcliffe's tale so aided.

Last lives of the 1745 rising's doomed circle fill the final volume. Kilmarnock and Radcliffe both faced the axe for their Stuart loyalty. Their letters show love, faith, and grit at the edge of death. Thomson's three volumes end as they began, keen to give the Jacobites their due from a fairer age.
22069-the-works-of-guy-de-maupassant-vol:
Guy de Maupassant wrote more perfect short stories than any Frenchman of his century. This eighth volume of his collected works in English shows his range. It opens with his famous essay on the novel. After reading Manon Lescaut, Don Quixote, Werther, Clarissa, Candide, and Madame Bovary, he asks, what may a novelist still attempt? The essay answers with Maupassant's own creed of truth seen through one temperament.

Stories fill the rest of the volume in his clear, hard style. Peasants, clerks, soldiers, and Parisian lovers pass under his cold eye. Maupassant died at forty-two, leaving some three hundred tales. This volume, essay included, is a strong place to meet him.
22086-the-son-of-monte-cristo-volume-ii:
Volume II of The Son of Monte-Cristo carries the sequel to Dumas's great romance toward its end. Spero, the Count's son, sleeps while the household gathers in Fanfaro's dining room. Monte-Cristo, Albert de Morcerf, Miss Clary, and Madame Caraman are all present. They have come to hear Fanfaro tell the story of his adventures.

Fanfaro's tale fills the volume with escapes, disguises, and old scores settled. The younger generation must finish what the Count began. Love, honour, and vengeance pull the characters in opposite directions. Readers of the first volume get the promised payoff here, in the same high-coloured style that made the Monte Cristo sequel a popular success.
22477-wintry-peacock-from-the-new-decame:
D. H. Lawrence wrote Wintry Peacock for the third volume of the New Decameron. The scene places a man and woman among cart-shed shafts. The shed faces the road where they stand talking.

She looks down at the ground, a little sideways. A small black frown shows on her brows as she broods. Then she looks straight into his eyes without warning. He blinks and wants to turn his face aside. Her look was too near, he admits, searching him for something. The frown stays on her keen, sallow brow throughout. Lawrence builds the whole tale's tension from glances like these. Readers get his charged, spare storytelling at work.
2250-king-richard-ii:
Richard II, a king who rules by divine right and poetic speech, is deposed by his cousin Bolingbroke after seizing the dead Gaunt's estate. Shakespeare's history unfolds almost entirely in verse, as Richard moves from glittering arrogance to a prison cell where he meditates on his fall. The garden scene, with its talk of an unweeded realm, is justly famous.

Bolingbroke's rise is efficient and cold, and the play asks whether a bad king may still be a sacred one. Richard's final soliloquy gives the tragedy its soul. For lovers of Shakespeare's language, this is among his richest early achievements.
2257-king-richard-iii:
Richard, Duke of Gloucester, deformed in body and gleeful in villainy, murders his way to the English throne. King Richard III follows his rise through the deaths of Clarence, the princes in the Tower, and his own wife, as ghosts visit him before Bosworth Field. Shakespeare makes Richard the play's witty, confiding narrator, and audiences have loved to hate him ever since.

The women he wrongs, from Margaret to Elizabeth, curse him with a chorus of grief that gives the play its moral weight. Richmond's victory closes the Wars of the Roses on a note of order restored. It remains one of Shakespeare's most stageworthy histories.
2258-king-henry-viii:
Henry VIII's divorce from Katherine of Aragon and marriage to Anne Boleyn drive Shakespeare's late history, with Cardinal Wolsey's fall as its great arc. The play moves through court ceremony, trials, and christenings, closing with the infant Elizabeth and a prophecy of her golden reign. Pageantry and politics share the stage.

Wolsey's farewell speech and Katherine's dying dignity give the piece its emotional peaks. Authorship is shared with John Fletcher in part, yet the verse keeps Shakespeare's late music. Readers will find a stately, reflective end to the history cycle.
22849-the-history-of-tasmania-volume-ii:
John West's History of Tasmania reaches back to 1643 in this second volume. At the era of Tasman's discovery, he writes, Van Diemen's Land was already inhabited. The Dutch heard voices and a trumpet-like sound, saw smoke from fires, and noticed notches cut five feet apart in tree bark. They guessed at giants or at some unusual way of climbing.

West builds his colonial history from such early encounters forward. Settlement, government, conflict, and the fate of the island's first people all enter the record. He wrote as a participant in the colony's public life, and his judgments carry that closeness. The volume remains a standard early source on Tasmania, valuable and open to question in the usual ways of pioneer history.
2416-the-house-of-pride-and-other-tales-:
Jack London's House of Pride and Other Tales of Hawaii gathers stories set in the islands, from the leper colony of Molokai to Honolulu's drawing rooms. The title story follows a proud man whose secret unravels his family, while other tales treat disease, race, and the clash of cultures in Hawaii. London writes the islands with a visitor's fascination and a reformer's anger.

The collection shows London beyond the Yukon, engaged with empire and its human costs. Its stories vary from melodrama to sharp social criticism. Readers will find a different, compelling London.
4802-the-rise-of-the-dutch-republic-volu:
John Lothrop Motley, D.C.L., LL.D., opens this second volume of The Rise of the Dutch Republic, dated 1855, with the second part of his historical introduction. Chapter seven begins with five centuries of isolation succeeding in the Netherlands, as throughout Europe. A thousand obscure rills, Motley says, slowly prepare the great stream of universal culture, during five dismal centuries of feudalism.

In those centuries, he argues, there is little talk of human right or obedience to divine reason. Rights there are none, only forces, and three great forces gradually arise, develop, and act upon each other and on society. The sword comes first, for a time the only force, the force of iron. The land's master, having acquired property in territory and in the people who feed thereon, distributes it to subalterns often but a shade beneath him. Readers get Motley's sweeping introduction, before the narrative proper begins.
4812-the-rise-of-the-dutch-republic-volu:
In this eleventh volume, covering 1566, part two, Motley's Rise of the Dutch Republic presses on. Its file header numbers it as the twelfth Gutenberg volume, volume two, book one, of 1566. Chapter eight opens with secret policy of the government, Berghen and Montigny in Spain, and debates at Segovia. Correspondence of the Duchess with Philip, the king's procrastination and dissimulation, and a secret communication to the Pope follow.

The effect of the king's letters to the government, secret instructions to the Duchess, and Margaret's desponding statements join her misrepresentations of Orange, Egmont, and others. Philip's wrath and duplicity, Egmont's exertions in Flanders, and Orange's return to Antwerp lead to an agreement of September 2. Horn at Tournay, excavations in the cathedral, almost universal attendance at preaching, and Horn's difficult position carry the volume on. Readers get Motley's account of secret diplomacy and religious tension in 1566.
4814-the-rise-of-the-dutch-republic-volu:
Motley carries The Rise of the Dutch Republic into 1567, part two, in this thirteenth volume. Its file header numbers it as the fourteenth Gutenberg volume. Part three, Alva, chapter one, opens with continued dissensions in the Spanish cabinet between Ruy Gomez and Alva. The conquest of the Netherlands is entrusted to the Duke, whose birth, previous career, and character are sketched.

Organisation of the invading army and its march follow, with complaints of Duchess Margaret. Alva receives deputations on the frontier, meets Egmont, and is received by the Duchess of Parma. Circular letters require cities to accept garrisons, while Margaret's secret correspondence and universal apprehension grow. Keys of great cities are demanded by Alva, secret plans arranged before the Duke's departure take shape, and arrest of Orange, Egmont, Horn, and others is determined upon. Readers get Motley's account of Alva's arrival and the tightening Spanish grip.
4816-the-rise-of-the-dutch-republic-volu:
This fifteenth volume of The Rise of the Dutch Republic covers 1568, part two. Its file header numbers it as the sixteenth Gutenberg volume. Chapter three opens with preparations of the Duke against Count Louis, whose situation in Friesland grows precarious. Alva enters Friesland, skirmishing follows near Groningen, and patriots retreat.

An error by Louis and his position at Jemmingen follow, with mutinous demonstrations by his troops, partly restored by Louis himself. An attempt to destroy the dykes is interrupted by Alva's forces, and artful strategy by the Duke brings defeat of Count Louis and utter destruction of his army. Outrages by Spaniards, Alva at Utrecht, and execution of Vrouw van Diemen follow, with Don Carlos, fables concerning him and Queen Isabella, and mystery over his death. Secret letters of Philip to the Pope close the chapter. Readers get Motley's account of 1568's disaster in Friesland.
4827-the-rise-of-the-dutch-republic-volu:
Don John of Austria enters Brussels in triumph in 1577, but John Lothrop Motley quickly shows the hollow side of the ceremony. Secret letters between Don John, his secretary Escovedo, and Antonio Perez reveal plots, gloom, and plans for harsh measures, while Orange sets out his own views on peace, war, and toleration.

Negotiations at Gertruydenberg follow, with papers passing between the governor's envoys and Orange, and three rival parties forming in the provinces. Motley also notes the execution of Peter Panis for heresy and the death of Viglius. The volume captures a moment when ceremony hid distrust, and talks masked a return to war.
4828-the-rise-of-the-dutch-republic-volu:
In this twenty-sixth volume, covering 1577, part three, Motley's Rise of the Dutch Republic continues. Its file header numbers it as the twenty-eighth Gutenberg volume. Chapter three opens with the city of Namur and Margaret of Valois, whose intrigues in Hainault favour Alencon. Her reception by Don John at Namur, with festivities in her honour, precedes seizure of Namur citadel.

A plan for seizing Antwerp's citadel follows, with a letter from the estates to Philip, sent by Escovedo, whose fate in Madrid is traced. Repairing of dykes, the Prince's visit to Holland, and his letter to the estates carry the chapter on, amid a governor seizing strongholds while a French princess schemes for her own candidate. Don John's bold stroke at Namur, and Margaret's intrigues for Alencon, show how many players crowd the Netherlands. Readers get Motley's account of 1577's citadel seizures and court intrigue.
4830-the-rise-of-the-dutch-republic-volu:
Motley carries The Rise of the Dutch Republic into 1578, part two, in this twenty-eighth volume. Its file header numbers it as the thirtieth Gutenberg volume. Chapter five opens with towns taken by Don John, and wrath excited against the aristocratic party by recent defeat. Attempts upon Amsterdam, the Satisfaction of Amsterdam, and its effects follow, with De Selles sent bearing royal letters from Spain.

Terms offered by Philip, proclamation of Don John, and correspondence between De Selles and the States-General, and between King and governor-general, fill the chapter's middle. New forces raised by the States show provinces answering royal terms with their own armies, while Don John's towns fall and Amsterdam's settlement reshapes its allegiance. Motley follows diplomacy and war together, as Philip offers terms his governor cannot enforce. Readers get 1578's shifting towns, terms, and armies.
4831-the-rise-of-the-dutch-republic-volu:
Alexander Farnese takes command of Spanish forces in the Netherlands in 1578, and John Lothrop Motley begins with the man himself: his birth, schooling, marriage, and early exploits at Lepanto and Gemblours. The portrait gives way to a country torn by foreign troops, as Anjou lingers at Mons, John Casimir intrigues at Ghent, and rival armies ravage the land.

Orange answers the anarchy with a new pacification and a religious peace at Ghent, calming riots and image-breaking that had angered even his friends. Elizabeth's remonstrances run through the story as well. Motley blends biography with civil war, showing how one commander's arrival changed a conflict already sliding toward chaos.
6152-athens-its-rise-and-fall-book-ii:
Edward Bulwer Lytton's second book of Athens runs from Solon's legislation to Marathon, 594 to 490 BC. Its chapters treat Cylon's conspiracy, loss of Salamis, Solon's first appearance, success against Megara, the Cirrhaean war, Epimenides, and the political state of Athens.

The opening detects the first symptom of crisis in Draco's laws of 621 BC, whose undue severity proved general discontent. Scarcely had those laws passed when conspiracy broke against the oligarchy under Megacles of the Alcmaeonic house. This book alone is described here, tracing Athens from oligarchy toward popular power. Solon's laws and character anchor the book's middle chapters.
6153-athens-its-rise-and-fall-book-iii:
Edward Bulwer Lytton's third book of Athens, in volume two, opens with Miltiades: his character and popularity, naval expedition, siege of Paros, accusation, sentence, and death. The Athenian tragedy follows, from Thespis and Phrynichus to Aeschylus and analysis of his plays.

Aristides, Themistocles, ostracism, and the silver mines of Laurion turned to naval increase come next, with Darius preparing, Egypt revolting, and Xerxes resolving on invasion. Envoys demand tribute, a bridge spans the Hellespont, and the Persian host reviews at Abydos. This book alone is described here. Miltiades, Aristides, and Themistocles share the stage in turn.
7029-book-of-etiquette-volume-ii:
Lillian Eichler's Book of Etiquette, volume two, opens with a tea table that should never be cluttered with things the hostess does not need. Published by Nelson Doubleday in 1922, with copyright 1921, the illustrated volume carries part three on servants. Chapters treat the servant in the household, words to mistress and to servant, how to address servants, and the child and the servant.

The invisible barrier, the servant who speaks, and the servants of a big house follow. Then come the butler, his correct dress, the second man, the chauffeur and his duties, the valet, the page, and maid servants. Only this second volume's matter is described here, as Eichler guides a household through service with order and courtesy.
7064-a-half-century-of-conflict-volume-i:
Francis Parkman continues A Half Century of Conflict in this second volume, opening at chapter fifteen with France in the far west from 1697 to 1741. French explorers fill the pages: Le Sueur on the St Peter's, Canadians on the Missouri, Juchereau de Saint Denis, and Benard de la Harpe on Red River. Adventures of Du Tisne, Bourgmont among the Comanches, and the Mallet brothers in Colorado and New Mexico follow.

Chapter sixteen searches for the Pacific from 1716 to 1761, through Charlevoix and the Sioux mission. Verendrye and his sons visit the Mandans, meet Snake Indians, and reach the Rocky Mountains before panic and return. Chapter seventeen builds the chain of posts from 1700 to 1750. Only this second volume's span is described here.
7167-the-guide-to-reading-the-pocket-uni:
Lyman Abbott opens this guide with a plain claim: books in a home may serve as ornaments, tools, or friends. He tells of a rich man who built a seaside house. Its shelves proved too shallow for plain books, a small joke on bindings that matter more than reading. Abbott then sets out how study and reading should work in daily life.

John Macy writes on the purpose of reading, Richard Le Gallienne on getting the best out of books, and Asa Don Dickinson on a guide to daily reading. Indexes of authors and titles close the volume, so a reader can find a book and a plan for it with ease. The whole book treats reading as a habit to shape, not a shelf to admire.
7169-ma-rkandeya-pura-na-books-vii-and-v:
Books Seven and Eight of the Markandeya Purana arrive here in the verse translation of B. Hale Wortham, first printed in the Journal of the Royal Asiatic Society in 1881. Book Seven opens with King Harishchandra, a saintly ruler pure in heart, whose just reign keeps famine, pain, and untimely death at bay. His people grow rich in good works yet stay free of pride.

Wortham keeps the old tale in English verse, holding the rhythm of a story told for moral force rather than for speed. The king's virtue sets the measure for all that follows, and the translation lets an English reader hear a Sanskrit purana in something close to its own storytelling voice. Both books stand as one linked telling.
7351-expositions-of-holy-scripture-st-ma:
Alexander Maclaren's Expositions of Holy Scripture take up St Matthew, chapters nine to twenty-eight, in a long series of sermons on single passages. Christ's encouragements, soul-healing first and body-healing second, the call of Matthew, and the touch of faith and the touch of Christ open the run. A Christlike judgment of men and the obscure apostles follow, with Christ's charge to his heralds and the widened mission, its perils and defences, close behind.

Like teacher, like scholar, and the king's charge to his ambassadors carry the exposition toward the Passion and its lessons. Maclaren preaches passage by passage, drawing doctrine and duty from each text with a preacher's warmth. The volume serves readers who study Matthew slowly, chapter by chapter.
7413-egyptian-tales-translated-from-the-:
Flinders Petrie's second series of Egyptian tales moves forward to the Eighteenth and Nineteenth Dynasties, the age of Egypt's empire. The first series had covered the Fourth through Twelfth Dynasties. This volume, first published in 1895 and reissued in 1913, continues the work of translating fiction straight from the papyri, with illustrations by Tristram Ellis.

Petrie's preface corrects a misunderstanding. Readers who hear simple ancient fiction may expect fairy tales of impossible beings. The Egyptian tales, he insists, are exactly the opposite: realistic stories that place the reader in a different land and age, or a different level of society. The volume thus offers not marvels for children, but the everyday imagination of a great civilization.
8414-freedom-talks-no-ii:
Julia Seton, a physician and New Thought writer, offers a second volume of Freedom Talks, following her books on concentration and marriage. Contents include The Secret of Healing, The Risen Self, Transcendentalism, Psychology of Insanity, The Law Eternal, and Perfect Liberty, with cosmic therapeutics closing the set. Seton's theme is freedom as a state of mind.

New Thought taught that thought shapes health and circumstance, and Seton, a doctor, argues it in plain, confident talks. Readers interested in the history of American mind-cure, positive thinking, and early psychology will find a clear, earnest example. The talks read as lectures for seekers, practical rather than academic, and sure of their message.
8519-the-life-and-voyages-of-christopher:
Washington Irving's Life and Voyages of Christopher Columbus continues in volume 2, in the author's revised edition of 1892. Contents of volume 2 open with book 11, on the administration of Columbus's discoveries, following the admiral through his later voyages, governorship, disgrace, and final years, with Seneca's Medea as epigraph.

Irving, America's first literary celebrity, wrote the standard Columbus life of his century, romantic and readable, from Spanish sources. Volume 2 covers the harder half of the story, after the first landfall, when colonies failed and courts turned. Readers get a classic biography, best read with modern scholarship alongside, for its view of Columbus as Irving's age saw him.
8885-the-works-of-aphra-behn-volume-ii:
Montague Summers edits this second volume of Aphra Behn's works, gathering four plays with notes: Abd elazer. Or the Moor's Revenge, The Young King, or the Mistake, The City Heiress, or Sir Timothy Treat-All. The Feign'd Courtezans, or a Night's Intrigue. Abd elazer opens with its argument: the old king of Spain. Having conquered Fez and killed the Moorish monarch, takes the orphaned prince Abdelazer under protection and makes him general. Abdelazer, courageous but bent on revenge, becomes the queen's paramour to gain influence, and she, lustful and wicked, joins him in poisoning her husband.

Philip, her second son newly returned, enters a court of murder and ambition. The other plays vary the Restoration mix of politics, sex, and wit: a mistaken king, a city heiress, and feigned courtesans in a night's intrigue. Behn, the first professional English woman playwright, writes boldly for the Restoration stage.
9057-unspoken-sermons-series-i-ii-and-ii:
George MacDonald gathered his three series of Unspoken Sermons into one volume. The sermons take their texts from the Gospels and the life of Christ. Titles include The Child in the Midst, The Consuming Fire, and The Higher Faith. Later pieces treat prayer, self-denial, and the truth in Jesus.

MacDonald writes as a pastor and a poet, not as a dry theologian. He urges readers to know God as a Father and to live by love. The sermons shaped many Victorian Christians and still speak to those who want faith joined to imagination and the heart.
9442-helbeck-of-bannisdale-volume-ii:
Mrs. Humphry Ward wrote Helbeck of Bannisdale in two volumes, and this second volume carries Books Three through Five. It opens amid tumult in an ironworks, where a foreman cries for women to reach their places. Four white-hot ingots blaze deserted on a truck, while men and boys push past in panic toward the furnace.

Helbeck, a Catholic squire, and his Protestant love face faith, family, and the industrial north in Ward's serious style. The volume deepens the novel's moral conflict. It remains a powerful late Victorian novel of religion and conscience.
9474-cameos-from-english-history-from-ro:
Charlotte Mary Yonge wrote Cameos from English History in 1873, for young readers past their first school histories. Rather than list bare facts, she paints short scenes of persons and events, from Rollo the Viking chief down to King Edward II. Her aim was to make the past stick in the mind, through strong scenes and sharp character. The book grew from pieces first printed in a magazine.

Cameos range from Norse raids and Norman dukes to kings, queens, and rebels of medieval England. Each sketch lingers on a key hour, so a reader feels the scene, not just the date. Yonge writes with clear moral sense and a fondness for brave, flawed folk. A reader gets a vivid first path into English history, told as a chain of human moments.
9625-buried-cities-volume-1-pompeii:
Jennie Hall's Buried Cities, Part 1: Pompeii, tells young readers how a Roman town was lost and found. Hall opens by asking children if they love to dig for hidden treasure, from arrowheads to graves. The book then follows Pompeii from busy streets to ash and silence, and to the diggers who brought it back. Drawings and photos from original sources fill the pages.

Captions by a fellow teacher guide the eye through streets, houses, and finds. Hall writes with clarity and warmth for school use. A reader gets a lively first history of Pompeii, and a tale of disaster, patience, and the thrill of discovery.
9634-sir-george-tressady-volume-ii:
Volume two of Mrs. Humphry Ward's Sir George Tressady picks up George's political and married life in mid-course. The volume opens on a hot June morning, as George seeks his mother's signature for the Shapetsky dealings, then heads to the Commons. His mother's drawing room, littered with notes, bills, and fashion books, sets the social scene. Photos of the Fullerton family crowd her table.

Part two follows George through Parliament, society, and a marriage strained by ambition and belief. Ward writes with care for motive, class, and the price of public life. A reader gets the second half of a major Victorian political novel, rich in debate and domestic drama.
9757-leila-or-the-siege-of-granada-book-:
Book two of Edward Bulwer Lytton's Leila, or The Siege of Granada, moves to the Christian camp and the royal tent of Spain. Ferdinand holds night counsel with trusted warriors, his pavilion blazing with purple and cloth of gold. Maps and papers cover his table, and his calm, imperial brow suits the brilliant chivalry around him. The king and a Dominican frame the chapter.

A visitor and a hostage enter the tent's councils, as war and faith shape the siege's course. Lytton stages Spanish power with pageantry and care. A reader gets the second book of a Granada romance, where a king's court proves as fateful as any battlefield.
9758-leila-or-the-siege-of-granada-book-:
Book three of Edward Bulwer Lytton's Leila, or The Siege of Granada, turns to Isabel and the Jewish maiden. Leila, gentle and luxuriously reared, is called from her fears to the queen's presence. Isabel, high-spirited yet touched by her age's superstition, leans toward mercy even where her faith backs persecution. Her voice alone checks Torquemada's fiery zeal.

The book sets Leila's fate against the Inquisition's tribunal, where suspicion of heresy brings suffering. Lytton paints Isabel as a queen whose heart softens her creed's hard edge. A reader gets the middle book of a Granada romance, where mercy and bigotry contend for a young girl's life.
991-a-theological-political-treatise-par:
Baruch Spinoza's Theological-Political Treatise continues in Part Three, covering chapters eleven to fifteen, with sentence numbers added by a volunteer. Chapter eleven asks whether the apostles wrote their epistles as apostles and prophets, or merely as teachers, and what the word apostle truly means.

Spinoza argues that the epistles are not in the same rank as prophetic books, and that faith and reason serve different ends. His inquiry, calm and learned, seeks to free scripture from superstition and the state from clerical rule. Part Three is a key stretch of his argument for toleration and free thought.
9972-the-dramatic-works-of-gerhart-haupt:
This second volume of Gerhart Hauptmann's dramatic works, edited by Ludwig Lewisohn in 1913, gathers his social dramas in authorized translation. Hauptmann, who later won the Nobel Prize, moved German theatre toward naturalism, putting working people and their speech on stage.

The volume holds three plays: Drayman Henschel, about a Silesian carriage driver; Rose Bernd, about a young farm servant; and The Rats, set among Berlin tenement dwellers. Together they show his range, from village life to city poverty. Theatre readers get a strong entry point to modern drama's founder. Lewisohn's translations helped English readers discover Hauptmann early.
a-half-century-of-conflict-volume-ii:
Francis Parkman's history of the French and English struggle for North America reaches its second volume here, covering the years from 1697 into the 1750s. Parkman wrote with a novelist's pace and a scholar's appetite for documents, and the volume forms part of his larger France and England in North America series. Its ground is the whole continent, from the St. Lawrence to the Missouri and the Red River.

French explorers push west, La Vérendrye's family hunts for a route to the Pacific, and rival forts rise along the chain of posts. The war chapters give the siege and capture of Louisbourg in 1745, the wreck of the Duc d'Anville expedition, and the Acadian conflicts that followed. Readers get narrative history at full stretch, driven by men, missions, and forts competing for a continent.
a-theological-political-treatise-part-ii:
Baruch Spinoza argues about Scripture, faith, and reason in part three of his Theologico-Political Treatise, covering chapters eleven to fifteen. The contents list shows the topics plainly. One chapter asks whether the apostles wrote as prophets or as teachers. Another asks why Scripture is called sacred and the word of God.

Later chapters say Scripture teaches only simple doctrines needed for right conduct, define faith, and separate faith from philosophy once and for all. The last chapter argues that theology is not the servant of reason, nor reason of theology. Spinoza writes calmly, but his claims about free thought were bold and risky.
al-masudi-prairies-dor-meynard-vol-ii:
The second tome of Barbier de Meynard's Les Prairies d'Or appeared in 1863. It continues his complete French rendering of the Muruj al-Dhahab of al-Masudi, the tenth-century Arab traveler and historian of Baghdad. The full French set runs to nine tomes, printed for the Société Asiatique between 1861 and 1877.

Al-Masudi's book is a world in one work. It holds geography, the histories of the Persians, Greeks, Romans, and Jews, and the deeds of the caliphs down to his own day. He mixes what he read with what he saw on his travels to India and East Africa. Meynard's notes steady the reader through the names. This tome is one link in that whole.
al-masudi-prairies-dor-meynard-vol-iii:
Tome three of the French Muruj al-Dhahab of al-Masudi came out in 1864, in Barbier de Meynard's translation for the Société Asiatique. Al-Masudi, who died in 956, had traveled from Persia to East Africa and read the books of many peoples. His Meadows of Gold is part history, part geography, part cabinet of wonders.

Readers of the whole work meet creation lore, king lists, the marvels of India and China, and the long story of the caliphate. Al-Masudi loves a good tale and tells where he heard it. The French version, with Pavet de Courteille, is the complete one in a Western tongue. This volume holds one stretch of that great road.
al-masudi-prairies-dor-meynard-vol-vii:
Barbier de Meynard published the seventh tome of Les Prairies d'Or in 1873. The book renders the Muruj al-Dhahab of al-Masudi, the Arab historian and traveler who died in 956. His Meadows of Gold gathers all he had read and seen across a life of travel from Syria to Ceylon.

In the full work the reader moves from the creation through the kings of the earth to the caliphs of Islam. Geography, natural wonders, and court tales are woven through the annals. Al-Masudi is curious about everything and credulous about some of it, which is part of his charm. The French notes guide the way. Tome seven brings the end of the set in sight.
al-masudi-prairies-dor-meynard-vol-viii:
The eighth tome of the French Muruj al-Dhahab came out in 1874, in Barbier de Meynard's version for the Société Asiatique. Al-Masudi, its tenth-century author, called his book the Meadows of Gold and Mines of Gems. He meant it as a feast of history and geography drawn from his travels and his reading.

Kings of Persia and Rome, the prophets, the peoples of India and Africa, and the caliphs of Baghdad all pass through his pages. He pauses for pearls, earthquakes, singing sands, and the habits of strange birds. The French text, made with Pavet de Courteille, is the complete rendering in a Western language. One tome remains after this.
alcibiades-ii:
Benjamin Jowett translated this short dialogue, and his appendix states plainly that it is by an imitator of Plato, not by Plato himself. It likely comes from the second or third generation after Plato, when his style was widely copied. Socrates finds Alcibiades on his way to pray and asks what he means to request.

The talk shows that men often pray for things that would harm them, since they do not know what is truly good. Socrates praises an old prayer that asks the gods to give good things and withhold bad ones, whether asked or not. The piece is brief, but its puzzle about prayer still feels fresh, as Jowett's notes observe.
athens-its-rise-and-fall-book-ii:
Book II of Athens: Its Rise and Fall, by Edward Bulwer Lytton, runs from Solon's legislation to Marathon. Its heading dates the span 594 to 490 BC. Lytton begins with the symptom of crisis. The laws of Draco were unduly severe. That severity, he argues, proves a general discontent. Harsh law rarely confirms a government. It usually strengthens a people against it. Scarcely were they enacted when Cylon's conspiracy struck.

Cylon, an Olympic victor married to the tyrant of Megara's daughter, seized the citadel on an oracle's encouragement and failed. Then Solon appears, first in the struggle for Salamis against the Megarians, then as lawgiver. His legislation fills the book's center. The strange career of the Pisistratid tyrants follows. Marathon closes the arc. The citizen militia Solon's city bred defeats the empire that swallowed Ionia.
athens-its-rise-and-fall-book-iii:
Athens: Its Rise and Fall, Book III, by Edward Bulwer Lytton, appears at the head of his history's second volume. Its contents open with Miltiades after Marathon. His naval expedition and the siege of Paros follow. Accusation, sentence, and death in disgrace close his story. Lytton then pauses the politics for a full chapter on the Athenian tragedy, from Thespis and Phrynichus to an analysis of Aeschylus, the soldier poet of Marathon's generation.

Aristides and the rising Themistocles divide the next chapter. It covers the ostracism, the vote that exiled men by potsherd. It covers the silver mines of Laurion. Themistocles persuaded Athens to spend their product on a navy. Then Darius prepares and dies. Xerxes resolves on the conquest of Europe. Book III is the history's hinge. Athens becomes a sea power just in time to need one.
book-of-etiquette-volume-ii:
Lillian Eichler's Book of Etiquette, Volume Two, continues her popular guide to manners for American readers. The volume opens with a tea table, properly uncluttered, and proceeds through the household, the dinner table and the social calendar.

Part Three treats servants in detail: the butler, the second man, the chauffeur, the valet, the page, the lady's maid and the nurse-maid, with correct dress and duties for each. Later chapters plan the formal dinner, with the American hostess at the centre. Readers curious about how 1920s America taught itself good manners will find Eichler practical, confident and full of period detail.
cameos-from-english-history-from-rollo-t: Cameos from English History, from Rollo to Edward II, by Charlotte Yonge. The historical sketches. This book preserves that history. The library keeps the document safe. Writers of history may cite it later. The paper lasts as a quiet witness.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-abstemii:
An abstemius cannot take wine without risking vomiting. Since Mass consecration requires both species, bread and wine, such a person is consequently irregular. St. Alphonsus, following Francisco Suarez, teaches that this irregularity is of divine law, so no papal dispensation covers it. The term also covers one with a strong distaste for wine who can still take a little.

That distaste alone is not irregularity, but a papal dispensation is needed to excuse wine at the chalice purification and finger ablutions. A decree of Propaganda from 13 January 1665 granted such a dispensation to missionaries in China, where wine was scarce. Heretics also imposed wine abstention at times, and Tatian's Encratites used water even in the sacrament.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-albert-ii:
Albert II, or Albrecht II, was the eighteenth Archbishop of Magdeburg in Saxony, the son of Gunther III, Count of Kevernburg, who died in 1232. He studied at Hildesheim, Paris, and Bologna and became a prebendary of Magdeburg cathedral young. He was consecrated bishop by the pope at Rome in December 1206. He entered Magdeburg on Palm Sunday in April 1207, and five days later fire destroyed much of the city, including his cathedral.

Albert laid the foundation stone of today's cathedral in 1208 and rebuilt much of the city, earning credit as founder of the Neustadt, the new town. He brought the Dominicans to Magdeburg in 1224 and the Franciscans in 1225, and founded a women's convent honouring St. Mary Magdalen. Beyond his diocese he played a leading part in the struggle for the imperial crown, shifting his support from Otto IV to Frederick II after Otto's excommunication in 1211.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-amalricus-aug:
Amalricus Augerii was a fourteenth-century church historian and Augustinian, doctor of the University of Montpellier, prior of a monastery of his order, and chaplain to Urban V in 1362. His learning was great, above all in church history. His offices joined scholarship, monastic rule, and papal court service in one varied career.

His chief work, Actus Romanorum Pontificum, runs alphabetically from St. Peter to 1321, edited chronologically in Eccard's Scriptores medii aevi, volume two, pages 1641 to 1824. An alphabetical pontifical history to 1321, it orders the popes for ready reference rather than narrative.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-anacletus-ii:
Anacletus II was the title taken by Cardinal Pietro Pierleone at the contested papal election of 1130, and he held it until his death on 25 January 1138. The Pierleoni ranked among the wealthiest and most powerful senatorial families of Rome, though men never forgot their Jewish descent or their rise through moneylending. Pierleone studied at Paris, became a monk at Cluny, and rose to cardinal-deacon of Saints Cosmas and Damian.

Most cardinals and nearly all the people of Rome stood behind him, and his rival Innocent fled the city. Yet Bernard of Clairvaux won nearly the whole Christian world for Innocent, judging his election purer, more regular, and earlier, and his character above attack. When Anacletus died, Rome preferred Innocent so plainly that his successor Victor IV soon submitted, ending an eight-year schism.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-antipope-john:
Antipope 997-998, died probably in 1013. After John XV's death, Bruno, Otto III's chaplain, became Gregory V, crowned May 996. In May the new pope crowned young Otto III emperor in Rome. After Otto left, Crescentius drove the pope from Rome in September 996. In May 997 Crescentius made Archbishop John Philagathus antipope, fresh from a Constantinople mission. John was a Rossano, Calabria, native, then Byzantine territory.

St. Nilus, John's compatriot, vainly dissuaded him. At Pavia's 997 synod Gregory V excommunicated Crescentius. That winter Otto III entered Rome in February 998; the antipope fled, Crescentius held Sant' Angelo. John was captured, blinded, nose and ears mutilated, and brought to Rome. Gregory V deposed him; at Nilus's plea he went from prison to a monastery. At Easter 998 Otto took Sant' Angelo; Crescentius was beheaded. The Annales Fuldenses date John's death 2 April 1013.

Pisan antipope, born about 1370, died November 1419. Cossa was among seven cardinals deserting Gregory XII in May 1408 to convene Pisa's council, which he led. Of an impoverished Neapolitan noble family, he took arms in youth, later forsaking them for the Church. Energetic and talented, he took a Bologna law degree and entered the curia. In 1402 Boniface IX made him cardinal; next year he became legate of Romandiola.

A 1412 Roman council drew so few it was prorogued repeatedly, condemning only Wycliff before dissolving in March 1413. In May 1413 Ladislaus invaded Rome's province; John fled to Florence, seeking a general council to end the schism. Deposed at Constance in May 1415, John submitted. Secular and ambitious, his morals not above reproach, yet his foes exaggerated gravely. As Cossa again, he was confined at Rudolfzell, Gottlieben, Heidelberg, and Mannheim until Martin V's election freed him in 1418; he did homage to Martin V at Florence.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-apostolici-mi:
Apostolici Ministerii is a bull of Innocent XIII, dated 23 May 1724, aimed at reviving church discipline in Spain. The primate, or chief bishop, and King Philip had reported that the Council of Trent's disciplinary laws were gradually falling out of use. The pope sent the matter before the Sacred Congregation of the Council and, on its advice, issued the bull, laying down rules for secular and regular clergy in Spain.

Leading points include tonsure, the first clerical rite, granted only where religion demands it, with each cleric assigned to a church. Seminarians attend the cathedral on feast days only, so study is not broken. Candidates for orders must be examined and shown to know enough. Ordination titles, or incomes, must be sufficient for decent support, and shaky benefices are suppressed. Priests with care of souls must also teach their flocks regularly.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-benedict-xii:
Benedict XII, born Jacques Fournier, was the third pope to rule from Avignon, profiled in the 1913 Catholic Encyclopedia. Born at Saverdun in France, he was elected in December 1334 and died at Avignon in 1342. A Cistercian monk and Paris-trained theologian, he rose through Fontfroide abbey and the bishoprics of Pamiers and Mirepoix before his election.

Reform was his chief concern. He sent absentee clergy back to their posts, revoked his predecessors' promised appointments, and attacked plural holding of church offices. He stayed at Avignon despite hopes of return to Rome, and in 1339 began building the great papal palace that still stands. Money for famine relief in Italy and for church repair shows the other side of his rule.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-benno-ii:
Benno II, bishop of Osnabrück, is the subject of this 1913 Catholic Encyclopedia entry. Born at Lünigen in Swabia, he died in 1088 at the monastery of Iburg near Osnabrück. Schooled at Strasbourg under the learned Hermann of Reichenau, he taught at Speyer after a pilgrimage to the Holy Land.

Skill in building made him imperial architect to Emperor Henry III, overseeing castles and churches across the empire. When the Rhine threatened Speyer cathedral, Benno's engineering saved its foundations. Later, as bishop, he long sided with Emperor Henry IV against Pope Gregory VII. He signed the deposition of 1076, was freed from excommunication at Canossa, and retired to Iburg, the monastery he had founded.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-boniface-iii:
Boniface III, pope for less than a year in 607, won from Emperor Phocas the decree that Rome heads all churches. A Roman deacon and son of John Cataadioce, he served Gregory the Great as legate at Constantinople from 603, winning Phocas's regard by tact and prudence. After a near-year vacancy he was consecrated on 19 February 607 and died on 12 November.

His decree against Cyriacus of Constantinople reserved the title Universal Bishop to Rome alone. At Rome he held a council of the Roman clergy with seventy-two bishops, forbidding any discussion of a successor during a pope's or bishop's lifetime. No steps for a successor could begin until three days after burial. The council's acts are lost, and he was buried in Saint Peter's.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-boniface-vii:
Boniface VII, born Franco, was an intruder pope whose two seizures of Rome ended in murder and mob vengeance. In June 974, after Crescentius stirred revolt, Romans jailed Benedict VI in Sant'Angelo and raised Franco in his place. The imprisoned pope was soon put to death. Within little more than a month, Count Sicco retook the city, and Boniface fled to Constantinople with the Vatican treasury.

After nine years of exile, he returned on Otto II's death in 983, seized John XIV in April 984, and jailed him in Sant'Angelo, where John died four months later. Rome endured him for over a year. After his sudden death in July 985, probably by violence, his corpse was dragged through the streets and flung beneath the statue of Marcus Aurelius before clerics buried it.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-eanbald-ii:
Eanbald the Second, whose birth date is unknown, died in 810 or 812. A Catholic Encyclopedia entry tells how he was schooled in the famous School of York as a pupil of Alcuin. Eanbald the First's death brought his election as successor. On 8 September 797, pallium from Rome in hand, he was solemnly confirmed as archbishop.

He helped Ethelhard of Canterbury win back rights stripped by Offa. In 798 he gathered his clergy in synod at Finchale near Durham and passed wise rules for church courts and the keeping of Easter. Some credit him with a book of decrees and with bringing the Roman Ritual first into the church of York. The entry is short, but it fixes a reforming archbishop in troubled years.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-edward-iii:
Edward III was King of England from 1327 to 1377, born at Windsor in 1312 and dead at Sheen in 1377. Eldest son of Edward II and Isabella of France, he took the crown at fifteen when his father was deposed, and married Philippa of Hainault in 1328. Tall, strong, and fond of hunting, hawking, and war, he won fame in arms but, the entry judges, cared little for his people's good.

His first years were ruled by his mother and Mortimer, until he seized power for himself. He fought the Scots, first with shame in 1327, then with victory at Halidon Hill in 1333, where he set Edward Baliol on the Scottish throne. Quarrels with France then drew him into the long wars across the Channel, including the Crecy campaign, which made his name across Europe.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-eugenius-ii:
Eugenius II was Archbishop of Toledo from 647 to 657. His father was the Goth Evantius and had served as a cleric in the Toledo cathedral. The office pleased him so little that he fled to Saragossa hoping for a monk's life. King Chindaswith forced him back to take up the see, and despite small stature and weak health, he proved a zealous bishop who reformed the chant of the Divine Office.

His surviving work was printed at Paris in 1619 from the edition of Father Sirmond. It holds poems on sacred and secular themes. It also holds his revision of Dracontius's six-day creation poem, to which he added a seventh day. A letter to the king lays out the whole plan. He also edited Dracontius on his own misfortunes and wrote a treatise on the Trinity, probably aimed at the Arian Visigoths.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-felix-ii:
Felix II was antipope at Rome from 355 to 358, more properly so called. When Liberius was banished by Constantius, Felix, archdeacon of Rome, took his place. Arian bishops consecrated him, though the Roman clergy had solemnly pledged otherwise. The Roman people stayed loyal to the banished Liberius.

Liberius returned in 357, and an angry crowd drove Felix from the city. He tried to seize Santa Maria in Trastevere, then was banished. He lived quietly at Porto until his death in 365. Later legend confused him with a martyr and gave him a saint's honours.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-ferdinand-ii:
Ferdinand II was Holy Roman Emperor and champion of the Counter-Reformation from 1619 to 1637. Born in 1578, he studied under Jesuits at Graz and Ingolstadt. He vowed at Loreto to banish all heresy from the lands under his rule. Crowned king of Bohemia and Hungary, he faced a united revolt at once.

Bohemian estates chose the Palatine Frederick V as king in his place. The White Mountain victory in 1620 restored Ferdinand's rule. He then imposed the Counter-Reformation across Bohemia, Moravia, and Lower Austria. Lacking independence of judgment, he leaned heavily on his counsellors for decisions.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-fossombrone-f:
Fossombrone, the ancient Forum Sempronii, is a diocese in Pesaro in Italy, suffragan to Urbino, named for Caius Sempronius Gracchus. Its district is rich in antiquities: the statue of Vertumnus, the Furlo Pass cut by the emperor Vespasian, and bridges of Trajan and Diocletian over the Metaurus. Near the pass, in 552, the Byzantine general Narses defeated the Gothic king Totila at the battle of Petra Pertusa.

After the Donation of Pepin the town stayed under Spoleto until 1198. It then passed under papal rule, held in fief by the Este, Malatesta, and Montefeltro families, with a brief rule by Cesare Borgia. Christianity came, tradition says, through St. Felicianus of Foligno. Notable bishops include the poet Giacomo Guidiccioni and the mathematician Paul of Middelburg. The diocese counted 20,050 people in 40 parishes, with a Capuchin convent and houses of women religious.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-frederick-ii:
Frederick II, German king and Roman emperor, was born to Henry VI and Constance of Sicily. Born in December 1194, he died in Apulia in December 1250. The Catholic Encyclopedia entry follows a ruler who cared for Germany mainly as a guard for his power in Italy. His reign turned on one idea: Italy could not be held without Sicily, and Sicily could not be held without the imperial crown.

That idea set him against the popes, who feared a single power gripping Italy north and south. Frederick bought peace in Germany with wide gifts to princes and bishops, gifts that later grew into their near-sovereign rights. He also promised a crusade, was crowned emperor at Rome in November 1220, and swore again to take the cross. Italian affairs stayed the hinge of his whole stormy reign.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-gennadius-ii:
Gennadius II, born George Scholarius about 1400, became the first patriarch of Constantinople under Turkish rule. A teacher of philosophy and judge under John VIII, he spoke for union at Ferrara-Florence in 1438, then turned, under Marcus Eugenicus, into its fiercest Orthodox foe. His later writings clash so sharply with his early ones that scholars once thought two men shared his name.

After the city's fall on May 29, 1453, Sultan Mohammed chose Gennadius precisely because he hated union, and invested him with crosier and mantle on June 1. The patriarch then settled the terms of Orthodox life in the empire, the so-called Roman nation. A notice he left on his cell door warned Romans that losing faith meant losing the city, a warning the conquest had just fulfilled.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-henry-iii:
Henry III, German king and Roman emperor, was born in 1017 as son of Conrad II and died at Bodfeld in the Harz Mountains in 1056. Gifted and profoundly pious, he mastered administration under his father while living much like a monk, subjecting his frail body to severe penances. He conceived kingship as religious: like David, the priest-king, he would rule God's universal state, and the Christian moral law governed his actions.

His lenient policy checked Bohemia in 1041 and made Hungary a tributary vassal, yet fostered opposition he never fully overcame. Determined to keep the Church pure and free of simony, he nevertheless held inflexibly to investiture and presided over synods. At Sutri in 1046 he repudiated three rival popes, an act that revealed the contradiction at his reign's heart and hastened the papacy's rise against imperial power.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-henry-viii:
Henry VIII, king of England from 1509, was born in 1491 as second son of Henry VII and became heir when his brother Arthur died in 1502. A precocious child heaped with secular titles from five, he married his brother's widow Catherine of Aragon nine weeks after his accession. He won popularity by executing Empson and Dudley, and, guided by Wolsey, made England a European power, joining the Holy League against France in 1512 and winning at Flodden in 1513.

Henry's early reign kept excellent terms with Rome: Julius II sent him the golden rose. His Assertio Septem Sacramentorum against Luther won him the title Defender of the Faith from Leo X in 1521. The portion read follows him only through these confident years, before the breach with Rome that would turn his attention to domestic concerns. It shows a gifted, masterful sovereign whom even admirers like Thomas More knew would brook contradiction in nothing.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-joseph-ii:
Joseph II was the Habsburg emperor who ruled from 1765 to 1790 and tried to remake his lands by reason. The son of Maria Theresa and Francis I, he was shaped by French Enlightenment writers and by Frederick the Great. As co-regent with his mother he handled routine and military business, then ruled alone after her death in 1780.

Joseph pushed central rule from Vienna, made German the official tongue, ended serfdom, abolished the death penalty, and taxed nobles and clergy. In church affairs he built Josephinism, treating the Church as a department of state under the prince. His haste, Frederick said, took the second step before the first, and much of his program failed.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-julius-iii:
Giovan Maria Ciocchi del Monte became Pope Julius III after a conclave that lasted ten weeks. The son of a noted Roman jurist, he had read law at Perugia and Siena and theology with the Dominican Ambrosius Catharinus. Before his election he served as Archbishop of Siponto and Bishop of Pavia. He also acted as legate of Bologna and the Romagna, and as the first president of the Council of Trent.

At Trent he defended papal interests against Emperor Charles V and moved the council to Bologna in 1547. The conclave split among Imperial, French, and Farnese factions, and only a compromise between the last two produced his election in 1550. He soon restored Parma to Ottavio Farnese, as promised in the conclave, but broke with Farnese when the duke sought French aid against the emperor. Julius then allied himself with the emperor instead.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-jus-spolii:
Jus spolii, the right of spoil, was a medieval claim on a dead cleric's property, at least what he had gained from office. Old canons barred clerics from willing away goods gained from their benefices. As those canons loosened, churches were stripped at an incumbent's death, and bishops seized abbey spoil, treating abbeys as cathedral offshoots. When the Western Empire fell, anyone present at a cleric's death felt free to carry off what he could seize.

Sovereigns claimed it over dead bishops, and lesser lords over clerics dying in their domains. Councils at Tribur (895), Trosly (909), Clermont (1095), and Lateran II (1139) legislated against it. In the thirteenth century Rome revived the claim, holding that goods of beneficed clerics dying intestate belonged to the papal treasury. France, Germany, Belgium, and Portugal never allowed it, while Naples bought it off with an annual payment.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-lamp-and-lamp:
Lamp and lampadarii covers the lamps of early Christian worship. Little proves a strictly liturgical use in the first centuries. Yet night services and catacomb meetings at Rome plainly needed light. Many small terra-cotta lamps survive, plain or stamped with Christian symbols.

With the Church's freedom under Constantine, great metal chandeliers with dolphin arms holding lamps became conspicuous in Byzantine worship. A homily of the Syrian Narsai, who died in 512, pictures the liturgy with smoking censers and shining lamps while deacons wave fans like watchers. Nearly every early Last Supper image shows a lamp over the table. A pilgrim about 550 saw at Jerusalem the very lamp said to have hung in the Upper Room, kept as a relic.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-leo-vii:
Pope Leo VII, a Roman priest of St. Sixtus and likely a Benedictine monk, was elected pope on 3 January 936 and died on 13 July 939. His birth date is unknown. He seems to have been raised to the Chair of Peter by Alberic's power. Alberic, prince and senator of the Romans, faced a challenge to his rule in Rome from Hugo, king of Italy.

When Hugo was besieging the city, Leo summoned Odo, Abbot of Cluny, whose sway with both men made peace possible. Alberic's marriage to Hugo's daughter Alda brought at least a brief understanding. Leo's Bulls are mostly grants of privilege to monasteries, especially Cluny. He also named Frederick, Archbishop of Mainz, his vicar throughout Germany to reform erring clerics. He barred forced baptism of Jews, while allowing their expulsion from cities if they refused Christianity.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-leo-viii:
Pope Leo VIII, a Roman layman and protonotary, was raised to the papacy by Emperor Otho I after the emperor illegally deposed John XII in November 963. Chosen on 4 December and consecrated Bishop of Rome on 6 December, he had received all the lesser orders in the meantime from Sico, Bishop of Ostia, in violation of canon law. When Otho left Rome, the Romans expelled him, and John XII returned, condemned him, and degraded clerics he had ordained.

After John's death in May 964 the Romans elected Benedict instead. Otho hurried back and retook the city. Leo brought Benedict to trial, tearing the pallium from his shoulders in July 964. If Benedict acquiesced, Leo may count as true pope from July 964 until his death in early 965. No records survive of deeds from that period, though he is said to have granted Otho rights of nomination and restored papal lands to him.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-napoleon-iii:
Napoleon III, originally Louis-Napoleon Bonaparte, Emperor of the French, was born at Paris on 20 April 1808 and died at Chislehurst, England, on 6 January 1873. He was the third son of Louis Bonaparte, King of Holland, and Hortense de Beauharnais, daughter of Empress Josephine. After the First Empire fell, Hortense took her sons to Geneva, Aix, Augsburg and Arenenberg.

The principle of nationalities drew him in youth, and with his brother he joined an attempted rising in the States of the Church in 1831. He failed in coups at Strasbourg in 1836 and Boulogne in 1840, yet his book Idees Napoleoniennes cast him as his uncle's testamentary heir and a bold social reformer. Elected president in 1848, he seized power in 1851, became emperor in 1852, and fell after Sedan in 1870, dying in exile.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-otto-ii:
Otto II, king of the Germans and emperor of Rome, was son of Otto I and Adelaide, born in 955 and dead at Rome on 7 December 983. Elected king at Worms in 961 and crowned at Aix on 26 May, he was frail in body but bold and wilful in spirit. With him began a grand imperial policy that sought to restore the old world's bounds, with Germany and Italy holding the balance of power round the Mediterranean.

Ducal particularism pushed back hard. In Bavaria, Duchess Judith ruled as regent for her son Henry, called the Quarrelsome, who lost his duchy after backing rivals against Otto's grants to Swabia and the Eastmark. In 978 Lothair of France invaded Lorraine and sacked Aix, and Otto's later Italian ventures ended in defeat. The entry follows his wars, his court, and his short reign's turn toward empire.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-otto-iii:
Otto III, German king and Roman emperor, was born in 980 and died at Paterno on 24 January 1002. Elected king at Verona at the age of three, in restless times, he was claimed as ward by Henry the Quarrelsome. The deposed Duke of Bavaria wanted the imperial crown, and allied with Lothair of France. Willigis, Archbishop of Mainz, led Otto's party and won the boy's release, with Henry's duchy restored in return.

Otto's mother Theophano then ruled as regent, dropping her husband's imperial dreams to bind Church and State in a broad national policy. She kept feudal sway over Bohemia, styled herself emperor in Italy, and watched France slip free under Hugh Capet. After her death the weaker Adelaide held the regency, Slavs rose in the east, and the young emperor's own Roman visions and early death close the entry.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-paschal-iii: Paschal III, born Guido of Crema, was the second antipope of Alexander III's reign. He was elected in 1164 to follow Cardinal Octavian, who as Victor IV had warred for years against Alexander III. To please Frederick Barbarossa, Paschal canonized Charlemagne in 1165, but the Church never ratified that act. He died in 1168.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-pelagius-ii:
Pelagius II was pope from 579 to 590, taking office while Lombard armies ringed Rome. A Roman of Gothic descent and the son of Winigild, he waited four months for consecration. He hoped the emperor would confirm his election, but the blockade made waiting impossible. This Catholic Encyclopedia life sets his short pontificate inside two crises: Lombard pressure on Italy and the Istrian schism over the Three Chapters.

His chief moves were diplomatic. He sent envoys to Constantinople, with the deacon Gregory among them. He begged the Frankish kings, through Bishop Aunacharius of Auxerre, to strike at the Lombards. Around 584 he welcomed a new exarch from the East, though the troops he brought were too few. The entry also follows his letters pressing the Istrian bishops back toward Rome.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-philip-ii:
Philip II, called Augustus, was king of France from 1180 to 1223, son of Louis VII and Alix of Champagne. Born in 1165 and saved as a child after his father's pilgrimage to Becket's tomb, he took the throne in September 1180. Marriage to Isabella of Hainault and the deaths of Flanders's count and countess enlarged royal power in the north. His alliance with Henry II's sons brought the Treaty of Azay in 1189.

Struggle with the Plantagenets ruled his whole policy. He joined Richard Lionheart on the Third Crusade, quarrelled with him in Palestine, accused him of attempted poisoning, and conspired with John Lackland while Richard lay prisoner to Henry VI. After years of war, Bouvines on 27 July 1214, where Ferrand of Flanders was captured, counted as France's first national victory. He died at Mantes in 1223.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-pope-adrian-i:
Pope Adrian II reigned from 867 to 872, elected much against his will after the death of Saint Nicholas I. The venerable cardinal, now seventy-five, was beloved for charity and amiability and came from a Roman family that had already given the Church Stephen III and Sergius II. Twice before he had refused the dignity, and he had been married before taking orders.

As pope he followed his energetic predecessor closely. He strove for peace among Charlemagne's greedy descendants. He admitted the repentant King Lothair of Lorraine to communion at Monte Cassino after a public oath. He upheld bishops' right of appeal to Rome against Hincmar of Reims. At the Eighth General Council at Constantinople in 869 he deposed Photius and restored East-West unity, and he backed Cyril and Methodius and their Slavonic liturgy.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-pope-agapetus:
Pope Agapetus II, Roman-born, took office 10 May 946 and ruled ten years in what the entry calls the papacy's lowest humiliation. Temporal power had all but disappeared, and Alberic, vigorous Princeps and Senator, governed Rome, a model for later Italian tyrants. Even so, Christians everywhere honoured Agapetus's name and virtues.

He strove to bring back discipline to churches and cloisters and calmed unrest in the metropolitan see of Reims. He supported Otto the Great's design to convert the northern pagans and joined Italian nobles pressing Otto's first Italian campaign to end the peninsula's anarchy. Alberic's son Octavian, afterwards John XII, already stood fixed as successor, and Agapetus died in August 956 with a spotless name.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-pope-alexande:
Pope Alexander II reigned from 1061 to 1073, rising as Anselm of Lucca, a leader of the reform party. Born at Baggio of noble parentage, he drank in Cluny's reforming zeal with Hildebrand. At Milan he helped found the Pataria, the agitation against simony, the buying of church office, and clerical incontinence, lending it his eloquence and birth.

Sent to the emperor's court to silence him, he instead spread reform in Germany, and in 1057 the emperor made him bishop of Lucca. Twice he returned to Milan as papal legate with Hildebrand and Saint Peter Damian. On Nicholas II's death the cardinals elected him, while imperial and Lombard foes backed Cadalus of Parma, and the contest over papal election rights shaped his whole reign.

Pope Alexander III reigned from 1159 to 1181, born Orlando Bandinelli of a distinguished Sienese family. As a professor at Bologna he won fame as a canonist with his commentary on Gratian's Decretum, known as the Summa of Master Roland. Called to Rome by Eugenius III in 1150, he rose to cardinal deacon, cardinal priest of Saint Mark, and papal chancellor.

Adrian IV leaned on his counsel, and he animated the cardinals' independence party, which sought escape from the German yoke through alliance with the Normans of Naples. At Besançon in 1157 he told Barbarossa that imperial dignity was a papal beneficium, a favour, and nearly died under Otto of Wittelsbach's axe. After Adrian's death all but three of twenty-two cardinals elected him, while the imperial minority chose Octavian as Victor IV, launching a long schism.

Pope Alexander VII, born Fabio Chigi at Siena on 13 February 1599, was elected on 7 April 1655 and died at Rome on 22 May 1667. His father, nephew of Paul V, gave him a careful training, with his mother shaping his youth. Ill-health from an infant apoplexy kept him from school, but tutors drew out his precocity and love of reading.

He took doctorates in philosophy, law, and theology at Siena in his twenty-seventh year and entered church service at Rome in 1626. He served as vice-legate of Ferrara, Inquisitor of Malta, nuncio at Cologne, and envoy to the Münster conference that produced the Peace of Westphalia in 1648. Innocent X made him secretary of state in 1651 and cardinal in 1652. The eighty-day conclave of 1655 elected him unanimously as a foe of nepotism. Within a year he disappointed that hope by bringing his brother and nephews to Rome.

Pope Alexander VIII, born Pietro Ottoboni at Venice in April 1610, was elected on 5 October 1689 and died at Rome on 1 February 1691. Son of Marco Ottoboni, chancellor of the Venetian Republic, he studied brilliantly at Padua, taking doctorates in canon and civil law in 1627. He governed Terni, Rieti, and Spoleto, served fourteen years as auditor of the Rota, and became cardinal in 1652 and bishop of Brescia.

Already an octogenarian at his election, he lived only sixteen months, in which little of moment was done. Louis XIV, whose position was now critical, restored Avignon to him and renounced the abused right of asylum for the French embassy. Yet Alexander still declared the Gallican Declaration of 1682 null in August 1690, aided Venice against the Turks, bought Queen Christina's books for the Vatican, and condemned the doctrine of philosophical sin.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-pope-anastasi: Pope Anastasius II, a native of Rome, was elected on 24 November 496 and died on 16 November 498. His congratulatory letter to Clovis on his conversion is now judged a seventeenth-century forgery. He insisted that the name of Acacius, Patriarch of Constantinople, be struck from the diptychs, the lists read at Mass. Yet he recognised the validity of Acacius's sacramental acts. That attitude displeased the Romans. He also condemned Traducianism, the teaching that souls are passed on by parents.
