Pope Anastasius III was the one hundred and twenty-third occupant of the Holy See, elected in September 911 and dead by November 913. He was a Roman, son of a certain Lucian. His reign was marked with moderation, but history gives no details of his life beyond that. The one recorded activity is his work in settling the ecclesiastical divisions of Germany. He succeeded Sergius III, who reigned from 904 to 911, and ruled at most about two years and two months.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-pope-benedict:
Pope Benedict III, a learned and ascetic Roman, son of Peter, died on 17 April 858 after a troubled election. On Leo IV's death in July 855 Benedict was chosen, and envoys went to secure ratification from the emperors Lothaire and Louis II. The legates betrayed their trust, backing the ambitious excommunicated Cardinal Anastasius, and imperial agents tried to force Anastasius on the Roman Church.

Benedict was insulted and imprisoned, but most clergy and people stayed true to him, and the agents yielded. He was consecrated in September or October 855 and admitted his rival to lay communion after a synod condemned him. He wrote to the Frankish bishops blaming their silence for the empire's misery. He curbed the lawless subdeacon Hubert. He welcomed King Ethelwulf and his son Alfred, and repaired churches damaged in the Saracen raid of 846.

Pope Benedict VII, birth date unknown, died near October 983. Under Sicco's sway, Rome's clergy and people picked another Benedict to follow Benedict VI: the Bishop of Sutri, a Roman, son of David, in October 974. Boniface VII challenged his authority, and although the antipope himself had to flee, his backers forced Benedict to seek Otto II's aid.

Once the emperor had him firmly in place, he moved keenly against simony's rising tide in the Church and to lift monasticism, then civilisation's cause. Answering Carthage's people, who begged aid for wretched Africa, he consecrated the priest James, sent to him for the task. His reign ran to about October 983, yet what we know of his works falls short of its length.

Pope Benedict VIII, birth date unknown, died 9 April 1024. First of the Tusculan popes, he was Gregory of Tusculum's son by Maria and John XIX's brother. A layman still, he was thrust onto Peter's chair by force 18 May 1012. After ousting a rival, he proved a capable, forceful ruler. On 14 February 1014 he placed the imperial crown on the German king Henry II, and stayed his friend ever after.

Italy's peace gained from his crushing of the Crescentii, his rout of the Saracens, and his pact with the Normans, new arrivals in the south. In Germany he dedicated Bamberg cathedral, stopped at Fulda, and won from Henry a charter upholding Charlemagne's and Otto's gifts. At Pavia in 1022 he and the emperor held a weighty synod against clerical incontinence and simony, and he backed Cluny's reform.

Pope Benedict XIII, born Pietro Francesco Orsini on 2 February 1649, was a Dominican friar-pope of austere personal life. Son of Ferdinando Orsini and Giovanna Frangipani, he entered the Dominican novitiate at Venice at sixteen. He did so against his parents' will, though he was eldest son and heir to his childless uncle, the Duke of Bracciano. Clement IX approved his choice and halved his novitiate.

Made cardinal in 1672, he kept his order's habit and rule. He chose the poor diocese of Manfredonia over Salerno in 1675. There he reformed clergy and people by visitation, preaching, and care for the poor. Transferred to Cesena in 1680, he left a memorial of apostolic work at Siponto. His pontificate, from 1724 to his death in 1730, carried the same pastoral zeal to Rome.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-pope-bl-urban:
Pope Blessed Urban II, born Otho of Lagery at Châtillon-sur-Marne about 1042, reigned from 1088 to 1099 and launched the First Crusade. He studied at Reims under Saint Bruno, became canon and archdeacon there, and about 1070 retired to Cluny, where he was professed under Abbot Saint Hugh. Sent to Rome at Gregory VII's request, he became Gregory's chief adviser and Cardinal Bishop of Ostia in 1078.

As legate in France and Germany he filled vacant sees with Gregorian loyalists, deposed the pope's condemned men, and anathematised the antipope Guibert at Quedlinburg. Elected unanimously at Terracina on 12 March 1088, he pledged to follow Gregory in all things: what Gregory rejected, he rejected, and what Gregory loved, he embraced. Entry to Rome was barred at first, and the Normans on whom he relied were at civil war.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-pope-blessed-:
Pope Blessed Eugene III, born Bernardo Pignatelli near Pisa, was elected on 15 February 1145 and died at Tivoli on 8 July 1153. On the day Lucius II died, the cardinals feared the Roman populace would force the new pope to surrender temporal power. They buried Lucius in the Lateran and withdrew to Saint Caesarius on the Appian Way. There they chose outside their body the Cistercian Bernard of Pisa, abbot of Tre Fontane.

Enthroned at Saint John Lateran, Eugene fled the rebellious city for Farfa, where he was consecrated bishop, and then for Viterbo. He was powerless before the Roman mob yet assured by embassies of all Europe's sympathy. A canon of Pisa cathedral and steward of its temporalities, he had followed Saint Bernard of Clairvaux as a novice in 1135. He later repeopled abbeys for his order before his sudden elevation.

Pope Blessed Victor III, born Dauferius in 1026 or 1027 of a non-reigning branch of the Lombard dukes of Benevento, died at Rome on 16 September 1087. An only son, he fled an arranged marriage after his father's death in battle with the Normans in 1047. After a second flight to Cava, he entered Saint Sophia at Benevento as Desiderius.

The life there was not strict enough, so he moved to Tremite and to hermits at Majella. Noticed by Leo IX, he joined Monte Cassino in 1055 and was elected its abbot in 1057. Stephen IX kept the abbacy in life and sent him as legate to Constantinople. As abbot he rebuilt church and convent, founded schools of art, and restored discipline to two hundred monks. His new basilica was consecrated by Alexander II in 1071. His fame as abbot, second only to the founder's, carried him to the papacy in 1087.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-pope-boniface:
Pope Boniface II was elected on 17 September 530 and died in October 532, in a pontificate opened by a double election. The Liber Pontificalis first mentions a pope's Germanic ancestry in calling him son of Sigisbald. He had served the Roman Church from youth and, under Felix IV, was archdeacon of considerable influence.

Felix, fearing a Roman-Gothic contest, gathered clergy and senators and solemnly conferred the pallium on Boniface, proclaiming him successor under pain of excommunication for dissent. Nearly all Roman priests, sixty of perhaps seventy, refused him and elected Dioscorus instead, fearing Ostrogothic influence. Both were consecrated on 22 September 530, but Dioscorus died twenty-two days later, leaving Boniface in possession, and a December synod secured his rivals' submission.

Pope Boniface VIII, born Benedetto Gaetani at Anagni about 1235, reigned from 1294 to 1303 as one of the great canon lawyers of his age. Through his mother he was kin to the Segni house of Innocent III, Gregory IX, and Alexander IV. He studied at Todi, Spoleto, and perhaps Paris, took doctorates in canon and civil law, and held canonries at Anagni, Todi, Paris, Lyons, and Rome.

He accompanied Cardinal Ottobuono to England in 1265, entered the Curia about 1276 as consistorial advocate, and became cardinal-deacon in 1281 and cardinal-priest in 1291. As legate he served with distinction in France and Sicily. After Celestine V's unprecedented resignation in December 1294, Gaetani was elected, having, the entry argues, advised rather than forced the hermit-pope's abdication and its legal constitution.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-pope-callistu:
Pope Callistus II, born Guido of Burgundy, reigned from 1 February 1119 to 13 December 1124 and ended the Investiture Controversy. Son of Count William of Burgundy and kin to nearly all Europe's royal houses, he became Archbishop of Vienne in 1088. He served as papal legate in France under Paschal II.

When Paschal yielded the Privilegium to Henry V in 1111, Guido led French opposition. At Vienne in 1112 he denounced lay investiture as heresy and excommunicated Henry. After Gelasius II fled and died at Cluny in January 1119, Guido was elected at Cluny. Henry V had set up the antipope Gregory VIII, but Callistus pressed on to settlement. The Concordat of Worms of 1122 closed a struggle begun under Gregory VII, raging for a quarter-century over who should invest bishops with ring and staff.

Pope Callistus III, born Alfonso de Borja near Valencia on 31 December 1378, reigned from April 1455 to August 1458 with one consuming aim: a crusade against the Turks. Of noble family, he first backed the antipope Benedict XIII, then mediated Aragon's return to Martin V. He became Bishop of Valencia in 1429 and cardinal in 1444, famed for mortified life, firmness, and prudence.

Constantinople had fallen to Mohammed II in 1453, and Nicholas V's efforts had achieved nothing. On election Callistus sent nuncios to every European court, begging princes to set aside jealousies. He sent missionaries to preach the crusade, raise volunteers and taxes, and win prayers. He ordered midday bells to remind the faithful to pray for the crusaders. Yet princes were slow: Frederick III shunned a cause that would aid Hungary, and bishops resisted the crusade tax.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-pope-celestin:
Pope Celestine II, born Guido del Castello of Roman Tuscany, reigned briefly from September 1143 to March 1144. A disciple of Abelard, he joined great learning to the name of a grave and upright priest. Made cardinal in 1128, he served as legate to France in 1140, where he angered Saint Bernard by protecting Arnold of Brescia.

Succeeding Innocent II on 25 September 1143, he at once lifted from France the interdict his predecessor had imposed over Louis VII's opposition to the rightful Bishop of Bourges. He died on 8 March 1144, on the eve of a serious conflict with Roger of Sicily, after a reign of about six months.

Pope Celestine III, born Giacinto Bobone about 1106, was the first Roman Orsini to reach the Chair of Peter. Forty-seven years a cardinal, he was elected on 30 March 1191 in his eighty-fifth year, being only a deacon. He was ordained priest on 13 April and consecrated bishop the next day, Easter, then anointed and crowned Henry VI of Germany as emperor and Constantia as empress.

The Romans would not allow those rites until pope and king helped them vent their wrath on Tusculum, which was levelled and abandoned to Roman vengeance. The aged pope has been blamed for that cruelty, though the entry lays chief responsibility on the emperor. Celestine's longanimity toward the violent young Henry, who imprisoned Richard the Lion-Hearted for a huge ransom, drew criticism, and only in 1193 were Richard's captors excommunicated.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-pope-clement-:
Pope Clement II, born Suidger, was enthroned on 25 December 1046 and died on 9 October 1047, after Henry III crossed the Alps to cleanse a Rome holding three rival popes. Benedict IX and Sylvester III stood for rival noble factions, while Gregory VI had bought Benedict's resignation, a bargain that bore the outward aspect of simony.

Gregory met Henry at Piacenza with all honours, then summoned the Synod of Sutri on 20 December. Benedict refused to appear and was deposed in absence, Sylvester was stripped of rank and shut in a monastery, and Gregory, pleading only good intentions, deposed himself. The synod adjourned to Rome on 23 and 24 December, declared the chair vacant, and Henry's candidate Suidger took the name Clement II.

Pope Clement III, born Paolo Scolari, was elected on 19 December 1187 and died on 27 March 1191, one of five popes between Alexander III and Innocent III. He was Cardinal-Bishop of Palestrina and a Roman by birth, the first native Roman raised to the papacy since the rebellion in Arnold of Brescia's days. His mildness and love of peace turned Roman thoughts toward reconciliation.

Overtures produced a formal treaty securing both papal sovereignty and municipal liberties, and in February he entered the city amid boundless enthusiasm. From the Lateran he organised the Third Crusade, dispatching legates to reconcile warring monarchs and direct their energy to the Holy Sepulchre. At his death, just before Acre's capture, prospects still seemed bright despite Barbarossa's drowning and Philip Augustus's return, though William II of Sicily's death opened a fresh Hohenstaufen quarrel.

Pope Clement VII, born Giulio de' Medici in 1478, reigned from 1523 to 1534 through the sack of Rome and Henry VIII's divorce crisis. Born months after his father Giuliano's murder in the Pazzi conspiracy, he was declared legitimate through his parents' betrothal and raised by his uncle Lorenzo the Magnificent. Knight of Rhodes and Grand Prior of Capua, he became cardinal in September 1513 on his cousin Leo X's election and drove papal policy through Leo's reign.

Chosen pope on 18 November 1523 after Adrian VI's death, he faced a situation of extreme delicacy. The entry doubts one man in ten thousand could have steered the bark of Peter through it. Trained in Italian diplomacy, he harked back on decisions and tried to treat with both sides. Within a year he made a secret treaty with France against Charles V, his backer, leading through the League of Cognac to disaster.

Pope Clement VIII, born Ippolito Aldobrandini at Fano in March 1536, was elected on 30 January 1592 after a stormy conclave and died at Rome on 5 March 1605. Of a distinguished Florentine family, he progressed in law under his jurist father, served as consistorial advocate, auditor of the Rota, and datary, and became cardinal in 1585 and grand penitentiary. A legation to Poland won him Habsburg friendship by freeing the imprisoned Archduke Maximilian.

Blameless from childhood and directed for thirty years by Saint Philip Neri, his confessor, he made Philip's spirit his own on the throne, Baronius succeeding Neri as his confessor. He visited every Roman church and charitable house, rooting out abuses. He founded the Collegio Clementino and the Scots College. He instituted the Forty Hours' Devotion and issued constitutions against duelling and for the inviolability of the Papal States.

Pope Clement XII, born Lorenzo Corsini at Florence on 7 April 1652, was elected on 12 July 1730 and died at Rome on 6 February 1740. Benedict XIII's saintly reign had left the Church's spiritual life flourishing but its finances ruined by rapacious ministers, with growing deficit and exasperated subjects. After four months the cardinals chose Corsini, the best choice save for his seventy-eight years and failing eyesight.

A Corsini on his father's side and a Strozzi on his mother's, he studied at the Roman College and Pisa, taking a law doctorate after five years. At thirty-three he resigned primogeniture and entered the Church, buying a prelacy for 30,000 scudi as was then customary and enlarging his uncle's library. He served as nuncio-designate to Vienna, treasurer-general, governor of Sant'Angelo, and cardinal from 1706, bringing tact and prudence to affairs that demanded them.

Pope Clement XIII, born Carlo della Torre Rezzonico at Venice on 7 March 1693, was elected on 6 July 1758 and died at Rome on 2 February 1769. Educated by Jesuits at Bologna, he took a law degree at Padua. He became referendary of the Signatura in 1716 and governor of Rieti and Fano. He served as auditor of the Rota and cardinal-deacon in 1737. As Bishop of Padua in 1743, he held a 1746 synod and formed his clergy through a remarkable pastoral.

His people called him the saint, an exemplary man who, despite immense diocesan and private revenues, was always without money from lavish almsgiving. He even gave away his linen. He accepted the papacy in tears, gauging the gathering storm. Regalism and Jansenism were old foes, and rising above them stood the party of Voltaire and the Encyclopedists. They called Christianity the Infâme and agreed that destroying the Jesuits must come first.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-pope-damasus-:
Pope Damasus II, previously called Poppo, was a Bavarian and the third German raised to the See of Peter. On Clement II's death in July 1047 the Tusculan faction, aided secretly by Boniface, Margrave of Tuscany, restored Benedict IX, who disgraced the papacy for eight more months before vanishing from history. On Christmas Day 1047 an embassy told Henry III at Pölde of Clement's death and begged him, as Patricius of the Romans, to name a worthy successor.

The envoys proposed Halinard of Lyons, fluent in Italian and popular in Rome, but in January 1048 Henry appointed Poppo, Bishop of Brixen, and ordered Margrave Boniface to escort him to Rome. Boniface first refused, citing Benedict, but Henry's threat reduced him to obedience. After Benedict's removal Poppo entered Rome and was enthroned at the Lateran on 17 July 1048, dying of malaria at Palestrina twenty-three days later.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-pope-eugene-i:
Pope Eugene II was elected on 6 June 824 and died on 27 August 827, after a divided election that crowned the Roman nobility's triumph over the clergy. Paschal I had curbed the nobles, who turned to Frankish power. On his death they secured the consecration of Eugene, archpriest of Saint Sabina, though a Roman Council of 769 had denied them a real share in papal elections.

As archpriest he had fulfilled his duties most conscientiously, and as pope he beautified Saint Sabina with mosaics and metalwork bearing his name, intact into the sixteenth century. His biographer paints him as simple, humble, learned, eloquent, handsome, generous, and a lover of peace. His election was a Frankish triumph, and Louis the Pious sent Lothair to Rome. Lothair recalled banished nobles and agreed the Constitutio Romana of 824, advancing imperial claims while checking noble power.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-pope-gelasius:
Pope Gelasius II, born at Gaeta in an unknown year, was elected on 24 January 1118 and died at Cluny on 29 January 1119. Paschal II's stormy reign had ended, and the cardinals, knowing Henry V had concerted with Roman nobles to force an imperial candidate, met secretly in a Palatine monastery. They summoned the aged chancellor, Cardinal John of Gaeta, from Monte Cassino and, deaf to his pleas, declared him pope.

John, of a noble family probably the Gaetani, had entered Monte Cassino young and served successive popes as chancellor. He had shared Paschal's captivity and shielded him from zealots who charged heresy over the Privilegium signed under compulsion. When news spread of an election without the emperor, Cenzio Frangipani seized Gelasius by the throat. He stamped on him, dragged him by the hair, and chained him in a dungeon. Romans rose and forced his release and enthronement at the Lateran.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-pope-gregory-:
Pope Gregory VIII, born Alberto di Morra at Benevento early in the twelfth century, was elected at Ferrara on 21 October 1187. He died at Pisa on 17 December 1187, after one month and twenty-seven days. The year 1187 saw Christianity in Palestine nearly wiped out. Saladin won Hattin on 4 July and took Jerusalem on 3 October. The news struck Europe and, it is said, broke Urban III's heart.

The cardinals elected their chancellor Alberto the next day. A Beneventan of noble family and education, he became a monk young, cardinal-deacon in 1155, cardinal-priest in 1158, and Alexander III's chancellor in 1172. He had investigated Becket's murder as legate to England and crowned Alfonso II of Portugal. Beloved for mildness, he sought reconciliation with Barbarossa. He issued crusade letters enjoining prayer and fasting. He travelled to Pisa to make peace between Pisa and Genoa, essential for shipping troops, when death overtook him.

Pope Gregory XII, born Angelo Correr at Venice about 1327, was the pope during the Western Schism, reigning from 1406 to 1415. Bishop of Castello in 1380 and Patriarch of Constantinople in 1390, he served Innocent VII as secretary and legate of Ancona, becoming cardinal in 1405. His piety and desire to end the schism moved the cardinals to elect him on 30 November 1406.

Before the election each cardinal had sworn to abdicate if elected, should his rival Benedict XIII do the same, and Gregory repeated the oath. He notified Benedict on 12 December and reiterated his readiness to lay down the tiara. Negotiations agreed a meeting at Savona, but it never took place. Benedict showed no intent to renounce, Gregory's relatives and Ladislaus of Naples worked against the meeting, and Gregory, pleading fear of capture, wavered. He created four nephews cardinals against his promise, and seven cardinals deserted to plan a council to depose the popes.

Pope Gregory XIII, born Ugo Buoncompagni at Bologna on 7 January 1502, was elected on 13 May 1572 and died at Rome on 10 April 1585. He studied law at Bologna, graduated as doctor of canon and civil law, and taught there, counting among his pupils the cardinals Farnese, Madruzzi, Pole, Borromeo, and Hosius. Paul III made him judge of the Capitol and referendary, and sent him as jurist to Trent in 1545.

He served as prolegate of the Campagna and Bishop of Viesti in 1558 before priestly ordination. He was deputy to Trent under Pius IV, cardinal in 1564, and legate to Spain over Archbishop Carranza's heresy case. Elected through Cardinal Granvelle at seventy, still strong and energetic, he put behind a worldly youth. That youth included a son Giacomo born at Bologna. He followed his holy predecessor in consciousness of his office. His reign is remembered above all for the calendar reform that bears his name.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-pope-honorius:
Pope Honorius II, born Lamberto Scannabecchi of parents at Fagnano near Imola, was elected in December 1124 and died at Rome on 14 February 1130. Archdeacon of Bologna, he was called to Rome by Paschal II for learning, became Lateran canon, Cardinal-Priest of Santa Prassede, and Cardinal-Bishop of Ostia in 1117. He followed Gelasius II into exile and, as Callistus II's legate to Henry V in 1119, laboured three years in Germany for reconciliation.

Through his efforts the Concordat of Worms, the Pactum Calixtinum, was sealed on 23 September 1123. The emperor renounced investiture with staff and ring and promised free elections. At its signing the cardinal sang High Mass in the open near Worms and, after the Agnus Dei, kissed the emperor and gave him communion. His election was stormy. Frangipani partisans proclaimed him over Teobaldo, elected, who resigned to prevent schism. Honorius doubted his election's legality until all cardinals acknowledged him days later.

Pope Honorius III, born Cencio Savelli at Rome, was elected at Perugia on 18 July 1216 and died at Rome on 18 March 1227. Canon of Santa Maria Maggiore, he was papal chamberlain in 1188, cardinal-deacon in 1193, and cardinal-priest under Innocent III. He had tutored Frederick II, ward of Innocent. Nineteen cardinals at Perugia, fearing schism amid Italian troubles, empowered Ugolino of Ostia and Guido of Praeneste to choose. They picked Cencio, who accepted reluctantly.

Consecrated at Perugia on 24 July and crowned at Rome on 31 August, he won Roman hearts by kindness. Already aged, his reign was strenuous. Like Innocent III he aimed at the Holy Land's recovery and spiritual reform, but by kindness rather than force. He at once urged Europe's rulers to prepare the crusade decreed at Lateran IV for 1217. He taxed pope and cardinals a tenth and other clergy a twentieth of income for three years.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-pope-innocent:
Pope Innocent II, born Gregorio Papereschi of Rome's ancient Guidoni family, was elected on 14 February 1130 and died on 24 September 1143. Canon of the Lateran and abbot of Saints Nicholas and Primitivus, he became Cardinal-Deacon of Saint Angelo under Paschal II and shared Gelasius II's French exile with his future rival Pierleone. Under Callistus II he helped draw up the Concordat of Worms in 1122 and was sent to France in 1123.

On the morning after Honorius II's death the cardinal-bishops elected Gregory as Innocent II, and three hours later other cardinals elected Pierleone as Anacletus II. Both were consecrated on 23 February, Innocent at Santa Maria Nuova and Anacletus at Saint Peter's. Deserted by the Frangipani, Innocent retired to his family's Trastevere stronghold. He then went to France by Pisa and Genoa, winning Louis VI and the bishops at Étampes, Clermont, and Würzburg. He crowned Lothair at Liège in March 1131.

Pope Innocent III, born Lotario de' Conti in 1160 or 1161 at Anagni, was a pope of the Middle Ages, reigning from 1198 to 1216. Son of Count Trasimund of Segni, nephew of Clement III, he studied at Rome, theology at Paris, law at Bologna. He became a theologian and a jurist of his age. Gregory VIII made him subdeacon, Clement III made him cardinal-deacon in 1190, and under Celestine III, a foe of the Segni, he lived in retirement at Anagni.

Elected at Rome on the day Celestine died, 8 January 1198, at thirty-seven, he accepted reluctantly. With the throne vacant since Henry VI's death in 1197, he restored papal power in Rome. He won oaths from prefect and senator, then extended his sway across Italy. He sent legates to reclaim Romagna and the March of Ancona from Markward, excommunicating him and driving him off. He wrested Spoleto, Assisi, and Sora from adventurers.

Pope Innocent VII, born Cosimo de' Migliorati of humble parents at Sulmona about 1336, died on 6 November 1406. He studied at Perugia, Padua, and Bologna, graduating under the jurist Lignano. After teaching jurisprudence at Perugia and Padua, he went to Rome with Lignano and entered the Curia under Urban VI. Urban sent him as collector to England, where he remained about ten years.

On his return he became Bishop of Bologna in 1386 and Archbishop of Ravenna in 1387, holding the latter until 1400. Boniface IX made him Cardinal-Priest of Santa Croce in Gerusalemme in 1389 and sent him as legate to Lombardy and Tuscany. Elected on 17 October 1404, his reign fell in the Western Schism, his rival being Benedict XIII. Like the other cardinals, he had sworn to lay down the tiara if needed to end the schism.

Pope Innocent VIII, born Giovanni Battista Cibò at Genoa in 1432, was elected on 29 August 1484 and died at Rome on 25 July 1492. Son of the Roman senator Aran Cibò and Teodorina de' Mari, he lived a licentious youth with two illegitimate children, Franceschetto and Teodorina, before taking orders and entering Cardinal Calandrini's service. He became Bishop of Savona in 1467, exchanged it for Molfetta in 1472, and was raised to the cardinalate the following year.

At the 1484 conclave he signed, like all cardinals present, an election capitulation to safeguard the electors' personal interests. The choice fell on Cibò, who took the name Innocent VIII in honour of his countryman Innocent IV. His success owed much to Giuliano della Rovere. His chief concern, praised for kindliness, was peace among Christian princes, though he became entangled with King Ferrante of Naples.

Pope Innocent XII, Antonio Pignatelli, born at Spinazzola near Naples 13 March 1615, died at Rome 27 September 1700. He joined the Curia at twenty, serving in turn as vice-legate at Urbino, Malta's inquisitor, and Perugia's governor. Innocent X sent him as nuncio to Tuscany, and Alexander VII dispatched him to Poland, where he settled troubled church affairs and brought the Armenians into union with Rome.

Vienna gained him as nuncio in 1668. Innocent XI named him Cardinal-Priest of San Pancrazio and Faenza's bishop in 1682, then Naples's archbishop in 1687. After Alexander VIII died, neither French nor Spanish-Hapsburg cardinals could push a candidate through, and a compromise chose Pignatelli 12 July 1691. His Bull of 22 June 1692, Romanum decet Pontificem, sworn by the cardinals, barred any future pope from raising more than one kinsman to the cardinalate.

Pope Innocent XIII, Michelangelo dei Conti, born at Rome 13 May 1655, died there 7 March 1724. Carlo II, Duke of Poli, fathered him. He studied at the Roman College and joined the Curia under Alexander VIII. Alexander sent him in 1690 to carry the blessed hat and sword to Venice's Doge Morosini. Tarsus's titular archbishopric and the Lucerne nunciature came in 1695, Lisbon's nunciature in 1697.

Clement XI gave him the Cardinal-Priest's title of Santi Quirico e Giulitta in 1706, then gave him Osimo in 1709 and Viterbo in 1712. Illness made him give up his see in 1719. After Clement XI died, a stormy conclave chose him 8 May 1721, and he took the name Innocent XIII for Innocent III, whose blood he shared. Soon he granted Emperor Charles VI Sicily and took his oath in 1722.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-pope-john-ii:
Pope John II, a Roman, son of Projectus, ruled from 533 to 535. He may not have been born in the second region, the Coelimontium, but he had served as priest of Saint Clement's Basilica on Mons Coelius's slope. He appears to have been the first pope to take a new name on rising, 2 January 533. Saint Clement's basilica still holds memorials of Johannes, surnamed Mercurius.

His predecessor's death left a gap of over two months, during which sacred things were shamelessly trafficked and even sacred vessels put up for sale. Senate and Ostrogothic court at Ravenna heard the matter. The Senate's decree against simony in papal elections, passed under Boniface II, won confirmation from King Athalaric, who had it cut on marble and set in Saint Peter's atrium.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-pope-john-iii:
Pope John III, a Roman called Catelinus, died 13 July 574. Anastasius, styled illustris, fathered him, and he took the papacy seemingly 17 July 561. Imperial confirmation took its time, leaving five months between Pelagius I's death and his consecration. His reign of nearly thirteen years fell amid the stormy Lombard invasion, and almost every record of it has vanished.

He seems to have been a generous pontiff, keen for his people's good. An inscription visible as late as the fifteenth century praised his bounty amid hardship. Salonius of Embrun and Sagittarius of Gap, two unworthy bishops condemned at Lyons about 567, talked Guntram, King of Burgundy, into believing their condemnation unjust, and took their case to the pope. Moved by the king's letters, John gave them back their sees.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-pope-john-vii:
Pope John VII, year of birth unknown, reigned from 705 to 707 and died on 18 October 707. Like many popes of Rome's Byzantine age, John was Greek by birth. His parents, Blatta and Plato, came of a distinguished house. Plato had restored parts of the imperial palace on the Palatine. After becoming pope on 1 March 705, John built a palace near Santa Maria Antiqua.

Before elevation, John managed the papal estates along the Appian Way. In that role he raised a monument, its heart broken, to a most loving mother and the kindest of fathers. He adorned Santa Maria Antiqua with frescoes and gave it a new ambo. He also built a chapel for Our Lady in Saint Peter's. Though learned and eloquent, and remarkable for filial affection, he was timorous. When Justinian II sent him the Quinisext decrees, with articles against Rome, John simply returned them.

Pope John VIII, a Roman and son of Gundus, reigned from 872 to 882 and died on 16 December 882. He appears as archdeacon of the Roman Church in 853 and 869, and as such became pope on 14 December 872. His election was opposed by Formosus, who remained in opposition throughout his pontificate. All modern historians agree that John was one of the greatest of the great ninth-century popes.

A year or two before he became pope, Saint Methodius, brother of Saint Cyril, who had died in Rome in 869, had been sent back to Moravia as archbishop. He was to convert the Slavs, with permission to use Slavonic in the liturgy. This displeased German princes and bishops, who had designs on Moravian independence. Methodius was seized and imprisoned in 871, and only in 873 did news of his treatment and appeal reach John. Though he momentarily banned Slavonic in the liturgy, he insisted on Methodius's immediate restoration.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-pope-john-xii:
Pope John XII, date of birth unknown, reigned from 955 to 964. The younger Alberic, after his mother Marozia's downfall in 932, ruled Rome absolutely. Before his death he made the Roman nobles swear in Saint Peter's in 954 that his only son Octavius should succeed him. After Agapetus II's death, Octavius, then eighteen, was chosen successor on 16 December 955 and took the name John.

Temporal and spiritual authority in Rome were thus united in one person, a coarse, immoral man. His life made the Lateran spoken of as a brothel. War and the chase were more congenial to him than church government. Defeated by Duke Pandulf of Capua, he saw Berengarius, King of Italy, and his son Adalbert occupy the Ecclesiastical States. In this dilemma he turned to the German king Otto I, who came to Italy with an army. On 2 February 962 Otto was crowned emperor by the pope.

Pope John XIII, date of birth unknown, was enthroned on 1 October 965 and died on 6 September 972. After John XII's death in 964, Benedictus Grammaticus was elected as Benedict V. But Otto I restored the antipope Leo VIII, raised in 963, and exiled Benedict to Hamburg. Leo died in March 965, and the Romans asked the emperor to send Benedict back as pope. Otto said no, and Benedict died not long after, in July 965.

Before the imperial envoys Liutprand of Cremona and Otgar of Speyer, the emperor's man John, Bishop of Narni, won election as pope. His crowning as John XIII came on 1 October 965. Theodora's family was his own: by marriage to Senator Theophylactus she had, besides Marozia, another daughter, Theodora. She wed the consul John. Their marriage produced two daughters and three sons, John among them, later Bishop of Narni.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-pope-john-xvi:
Pope John XVII, birth date unknown, died 6 November 1003. Sylvester II's death on 12 May 1003 left no real power in Rome to check the nobles. The Crescentius faction regained the upper hand, and John Crescentius, son of the patricius whom Otto III had beaten and executed, took power himself. The next three popes owed their rise to him and bowed to his dominance.

Sicco, a Roman, won election first and consecration 13 June as John XVII, yet died 6 November. Before ordination he had married and fathered three sons, all churchmen too. Nothing survives of his doings across his few months as pope.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-pope-john-xxi:
Pope John XXII, Jacques d'Euse, born at Cahors in 1249, took the throne 5 September 1316 and died at Avignon 4 December 1334. Dominicans taught him at home; Montpellier and Paris gave him theology and law. He lectured at Toulouse and Cahors in canon law and civil law and befriended Charles II of Naples. Charles's backing won him Fréjus's bishopric in 1300.

Charles II's chancellor he became in 1309, moving to Avignon in 1310. He backed the Templars' suppression in legal opinions while defending Boniface VIII and Unam Sanctam. Clement V raised him to Cardinal-Bishop of Porto 23 December 1312. Clement's death on 20 April 1314 left the Holy See empty for two years and three and a half months. Carpentras's cardinals split into factions and could not agree. Once Philip V wore the crown, twenty-three cardinals gathered at Lyons 26 June 1316. Jacques won election 7 August.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-pope-julius-i:
Giuliano della Rovere was born at Albissola near Savona in 1443. His family was noble but poor. His uncle, Pope Sixtus IV, drew him into church life. Sixtus made him a cardinal in 1471. He then piled up bishoprics across France and Italy. Much of his income went to palaces, forts, and art.

He became pope as Julius II in 1503. At once he turned soldier-statesman. He marched at the head of his own troops in 1506. Perugia and Bologna returned to papal rule under him. He also wrested towns of the Romagna from Venice and Cesare Borgia. The entry follows his quarrels with France, his councils, and his patronage. It closes with his death at Rome in February 1513.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-pope-leo-xii:
Annibale della Genga was born at the family castle near Spoleto in 1760. He trained at Osimo and Rome. He was ordained priest at twenty-three after a dispensation for his youth. Pius VII noticed the handsome young cleric. He served as nuncio, or papal envoy, at Lucerne and Cologne. He also went on missions to Paris. Later he retired to the abbey of Monticelli. There he taught peasants to sing chant.

After Napoleon's fall he returned to diplomacy. He bore papal congratulations to Louis XVIII in Paris. The mission annoyed the powerful secretary of state Consalvi. The entry traces his later rise to the papacy. His reign closed with his death at Rome in February 1829.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-pope-leo-xiii:
Gioacchino Pecci was born at Carpineto in 1810. He was the sixth of seven sons. He won a reputation for fine Latin and Italian. He gained it during Jesuit schooling at Viterbo and Rome. After doctorates and legal studies he was ordained in 1837. He had helped Cardinal Sala run Rome's hospitals during a cholera outbreak. He went on to govern Benevento.

He was elected pope in 1878. Leo dealt with Bismarck's Germany. He faced broken relations with Belgium over schools. He saw slow gains for the church in Switzerland and Russia. The long entry follows his diplomacy across Europe. It notes his admired official writings and poems. His reign lasted twenty-five years. It ended with his death in July 1903.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-pope-lucius-i:
Gherardo Caccianemici was a canon regular from Bologna. He became cardinal-priest of Santa Croce in 1124. He served repeatedly as papal legate in Germany. There he helped elect King Lothair III. He backed Innocent II against the antipope Anacletus. Late in Innocent's reign he became papal chancellor and librarian.

He was elected pope at Rome in March 1144. Lucius tried to settle with King Roger of Sicily at Ceperano. He dissolved a Roman senate that had seized temporal power. A revived republican faction then rose against him. He marched on the Capitol against it. He was hurt by thrown stones. He died days later in February 1145.

Ubaldo Allucingoli came from Lucca. He was made cardinal-priest in 1141. He later became bishop of Ostia. He helped broker the 1177 peace of Venice. That peace settled Alexander III with Emperor Frederick I. Allucingoli was elected at Velletri in September 1181. His reign was spent largely outside Rome. Roman factions drove him out twice. They resented his refusal of their demands.

From Velletri, Segni, Bologna, and Verona he acted widely. He canonized Bruno of Segni. He sent Scotland's king the Golden Rose after lifting his excommunication. He consecrated Bologna's cathedral. He joined Frederick at a Verona synod. That synod cracked down on Cathars, Waldensians, and Arnoldists. Relations with the emperor stayed strained to his death in 1185.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-pope-marcellu:
Marcello Cervini was born at Montepulciano in 1501. His father was the papal treasurer of Ancona. Cervini studied at Siena and Rome. He won regard for clean living and learning. Paul III made him papal secretary. He advised the young Cardinal Farnese. He became cardinal-priest in 1539. He travelled on embassies to Charles V and Francis I.

He was one of three presidents of the Council of Trent from 1545. There he defended papal interests against the emperor's anger. He later guarded the Vatican Library. The entry ends with his election and short reign in 1555. It closes with his death at Rome on 6 May of that year.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-pope-marinus-:
Marinus II was a Roman cardinal of St Ciriacus. He reigned from 942 to 946. He was one of the popes put on the throne by Alberic. Alberic was Prince of the Romans. Though virtuous, Marinus dared not act without Alberic's leave. He left little mark on the wider world.

Quietly, he pushed reform abroad through legates. At home he worked by his own exertions. He favoured the monastic renewal spreading from Cluny. He repaired basilicas and cared for the poor. He died in April or May 946. He left a record of modest, steady service rather than power.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-pope-nicholas:
Gerhard of Burgundy was born at Chevron in Savoy. He became bishop of Florence in 1046. He was elected at Siena in December 1058. The Tusculan party had irregularly installed Benedict X at Rome. Gerhard was backed by Hildebrand and Duke Godfrey. He deposed Benedict at Sutri. He was crowned at Rome in January 1059.

He hired Norman troops through Hildebrand. He fought Benedict's supporters with them. He sent legates to Milan. They forced clergy to renounce simony, the buying of church office, and concubinage. He pressed the great reform of papal elections. The entry presents a cultured, stainless pontiff steering the church through a contested succession.

Giovanni Gaetani Orsini was born at Rome around 1216. His parents came from the Orsini and Gaetani houses. Innocent IV made him cardinal-deacon at twenty-eight. The pope was grateful for his father's defence of Rome against Frederick II. Orsini travelled with the pope to Lyons. He served as general inquisitor and protector of the Franciscans. He helped elect several popes. He won his own election at Viterbo in November 1277.

Nicholas worked to free Rome from foreign sway. He won Rudolf of Habsburg's renunciation of the Romagna. He forced Charles of Anjou to give up the regency of Tuscany. He also forced him to give up the Roman senatorship. He issued a constitution in July 1278 to guard the freedom of papal elections. Nephews gained rich posts under him. He died at Soriano in August 1280.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-pope-paschal-:
Rainerius was a monk of Cluny. Gregory VII brought him to the papal court. He became cardinal-priest of St Clement's. He was unanimously chosen pope there in August 1099. He protested that monastic training had not fitted him for the age's crises. His colleagues ignored his protests. Once consecrated, he ruled firmly and prudently for eighteen years.

He kept Urban II's crusading work alive. He did so through synods and journeys across Italy and France. He carried on the policies laid down by Gregory and Urban. Those two minds shaped his reign. The entry treats his long pontificate as a key force in building medieval papal power. It ends with his death at Rome in January 1118.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-pope-paul-ii:
Pietro Barbo was born at Venice in 1417. His mother was a sister of Eugene IV. He trained for business. He entered church life when his uncle became pope. He rose to cardinal-deacon in 1440. He was known for generosity and a commanding presence. He was influential under three popes. He was elected in August 1464. Cardinals unhappy with Pius II had helped his cause.

Paul loved display. He staged splendid carnivals. He built the palace of St Mark, now the Venice palace. He revised Rome's statutes. He relieved the poor. He let all cardinals wear the red biretta. His suppression of the abbreviators' college drew bitter opposition. His move against the Roman Academy did the same. Platina answered with a hostile life of him. Paul also protected universities and printing, and collected art.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-pope-paul-iii:
Alessandro Farnese was born at Rome or Canino in 1468. His old Roman house clustered around Lake Bolsena. He learned classical Latin and Italian under fine tutors. He studied at Rome and in Lorenzo the Magnificent's Florence palace. There he befriended the future Leo X. He was made cardinal-deacon in 1493. He held cardinal's rank for over forty years. He rose to dean of the Sacred College. He was elected in October 1534.

Paul pushed reform of the papal court with vigour. He set commissions on abuses. He overhauled the Camera, Rota, Penitentiaria, and Chancery. That work cleared ground for Trent's disciplinary canons. He resisted the emperor's wish to settle faith by vague compromise formulas. He held that a council must state belief precisely. He kept a careful balance between Francis I and Charles V. He died at Rome in November 1549.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-pope-pius-ii:
Enea Silvio de' Piccolomini was born at Corsignano near Siena in 1405. He was the eldest of eighteen children. His noble family was poor, and he helped his father work their estate. At eighteen he entered the University of Siena. Bernardine's preaching in 1425 stirred him toward monastic life, but friends talked him out of it. He studied classics and poetry at Florence, then law. In 1432 he went to the Council of Basle as secretary to Bishop Capranica. There he joined the opposition to Eugene IV.

As pope he called the congress of Mantua in 1459 to rally Christian states against the Turks. Few delegates came. Venice stalled, France promised nothing, and German pledges of troops were never kept. The decreed war came to nothing. On leaving Mantua he issued Execrabilis, condemning appeals from pope to council. The entry follows his reign to his death at Ancona in August 1464.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-pope-pius-iii:
Francesco Todeschini Piccolomini was born at Siena in 1439. His mother was a sister of Pius II. His boyhood passed in poverty until his uncle took him in. The uncle gave him his family name and arms and oversaw his schooling. He studied law at Perugia. Right after his doctorate his uncle made him archbishop of Siena. In 1460 he became cardinal-deacon. Paul II sent him as legate to Germany, where his German served him well.

He stayed away from Rome while Sixtus IV and Alexander VI held worldly reigns. A man who knew him well praised his packed days. He studied before dawn, prayed in the morning, and gave audiences open even to the humblest at midday. He ate only an evening meal every other day. Elected in September 1503, he reigned just four weeks and died at Rome in October.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-pope-pius-vii:
Barnaba Chiaramonti was born at Cesena in 1742 to Count Scipione and a deeply pious mother. She entered a Carmelite convent in 1763, having foretold his papacy and sufferings in his hearing. At sixteen he joined Santa Maria del Monte's Benedictine monastery as Brother Gregory. He taught at Parma and Rome, became abbot of his monastery, then bishop of Tivoli and Imola, and cardinal in 1785. As bishop of Imola in 1797 he told his flock not to resist the invading French uselessly.

Elected at Venice in March 1800, he faced Napoleon's remaking of Europe and the huge church losses imposed by the Imperial Deputation at Ratisbon. He could not resist its execution. After Napoleon's fall, Consalvi pleaded vainly at Vienna for restoring the old church order. Separate deals followed instead: Bavaria in 1817, Prussia in 1821, and a fresh distribution of dioceses. He died in August 1823.

Francesco Xaverio Castiglione was born at Cingoli in 1761 to a noble family. He studied at the Jesuit school in Osimo and canon law at Bologna and Rome. He helped his teacher Devoti compile the Institutiones, then served as vicar-general at Anagni and Cingoli. Pius VII made him bishop of Montalto in 1800, then of Cesena. Under French rule he refused the oath to the King of Italy and was carried off to Macerata, Mantua, and France.

He became cardinal in 1816 and bishop of Frascati and Grand Penitentiary in 1822. France and Austria wanted a mild, temperate pope in 1829, and after five weeks Castiglione was chosen. His twenty-month reign saw Catholic Emancipation pass in England in April 1829, letting Catholics sit in Parliament. He died on 1 December 1830.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-pope-saint-le:
Leo II was a Sicilian, son of one Paul. He was elected days after Agatho died in January 681, but consecration waited a year and seven months, until August 682. The delay likely came from talks with Emperor Constantine Pogonatus over the tax popes paid the treasury at consecration. Constantine had promised Agatho to abolish or cut it.

Leo's chief act was confirming the Sixth Oecumenical Council of 680-681, held at Constantinople against the Monothelites. He told the emperor the decrees stood confirmed, then spread them westward. His letters to Spain's king, bishops, and nobles explained the council and called bishops to subscribe. He made clear that condemning his predecessor Honorius I faulted inaction against heresy, not heretical teaching. A Toledo synod accepted the council in 684, after his death on 28 June 683.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-pope-sergius-:
Sergius II was of noble birth, from a family that gave two other popes to the church. Schooled in the schola cantorum, several popes patronized him, and Paschal made him cardinal-priest. Under Gregory IV he became archpriest. At the meeting to name Gregory's successor, most accepted Sergius, but a mob tried to force the deacon John onto the throne. John was shut in a monastery, and Sergius duly won consecration, apparently in January 844.

A hostile edition of the Liber Pontificalis paints him as a glutton who left business to his brother Benedict, who grabbed money while gout left Sergius helpless and irritable. Other editions contradict that portrait, and the entry calls it gross exaggeration. Consecrated without reference to Emperor Lothaire, Sergius faced Louis's army sent to test the election. He pacified Louis and crowned him king. He died on 27 January 847.

Sergius III was a Roman, son of Benedict. His birth date is unknown. He backed the party against Formosus. Since that party lost, its writings perished, and most of what we know comes from his enemies. An enemy says Formosus made him bishop of Caere to bar him from Rome. He stopped acting as bishop after Formosus died. He failed to win election in 898 and retired to Alberic of Spoleto.

Romans jailed the usurper Christopher and invited Sergius to take his place. He was consecrated on 29 January 904. At once he annulled Formosus's ordinations. Claims that he murdered two predecessors and fathered John XI by Marozia are highly doubtful, resting on bitter foes. He shielded Ravenna's archbishop and confirmed new English sees. He backed the Greeks' fourth-marriage ruling for Leo VI while they struck his name from their diptychs. He restored the Lateran Basilica and died on 14 April 911.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-pope-st-adria: Adrian III, of Roman extraction, was elected early in 884. He died near Modena in the summer of 885 while travelling to the diet Charles the Fat had called to settle the imperial succession. He was buried at Nonantula monastery, where his memory stayed in local veneration. By Leo XIII's decree, Rome's and Modena's clergy celebrate his Mass and office on 7 September.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-pope-st-bened:
Benedict II was a Roman, son of John, and died on 8 May 685. Sent young to the schola cantorum, he stood out for Scripture knowledge and singing. As a priest, humility, love of the poor, and generosity marked him. He took the papal office on 26 June 684 after a vacancy past eleven months.

To shorten such vacancies he won from Constantine Pogonatus a decree on imperial confirmations, either abolishing them or making them obtainable from the exarch in Italy. He adopted the emperor's two sons by taking locks of their hair. He pressed Spanish bishops to subscribe to the Sixth Council's decrees and sought the submission of Macarius of Antioch. He restored many Roman churches and aided clergy, deaconries for the poor, and sacristans. He was buried in St Peter's.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-pope-st-felix:
Felix III reigned from 483 to 492. He came from a Roman senatorial family and is said to be an ancestor of Gregory the Great. Nothing certain is known until he succeeded Simplicius in 483. The church was still locked in conflict with the Eutychian heresy. Emperor Zeno's Henoticon, or Act of Union, aimed to reconcile Catholics and Eutychians but split the East into three or four parties.

Zeno had expelled Antioch's and Alexandria's patriarchs from their sees. Peter the Tanner intruded at Antioch, and Peter Mongus seized Alexandria. In his first synod Felix excommunicated the Tanner. In 484 he also excommunicated Mongus, an act that opened a thirty-five-year schism between East and West. Mongus won Acacius's favour by subscribing to the Henoticon. His reign ended in 492, with the schism still open.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-pope-st-grego:
Gregory II reigned from 715 to 731 and may be the greatest eighth-century pope. A Roman, son of Marcellus and Honesta, he was called Gregory the Younger in the West and Dialogus in the East, where men confused him with Gregory I. Placed young in the schola cantorum, he became subdeacon and paymaster under Sergius I, then keeper of the papal library, the first papal librarian known by name.

As deacon he accompanied Constantine to Constantinople and answered every difficulty Justinian II raised over the Quinisext canons. As pope from 19 May 715 he first repaired Rome's walls against Lombards and a rising Saracen threat, though a Tiber flood stalled the work. When Leo III's iconoclast decrees and illegal taxes reached Italy, Gregory resisted both, and appealed to Charles Martel when the exarch could not stop the Lombards. Charles would not come, but Italian fury at the emperor grew.

Gregory III's father was John, a Syrian. His birth date is unknown. Romans elected him by acclamation as he walked in his predecessor's funeral procession on 11 February 731, so great was his fame for learning and virtue. He waited over a month for consecration, presumably for the Ravenna exarch's confirmation.

On iconoclasm he followed his predecessor. Legates and letters went from him to remonstrate with Leo III, and he held two Roman synods in 731 condemning image-breaking. As practical protest he honoured images and relics, building an oratory in St Peter's whose inscriptions survive in the Vatican crypts. Leo answered with force, seizing papal lands in Calabria and Sicily and handing their church jurisdiction to Constantinople. Gregory confirmed the respective rights of Aquileia and Grado, and Antoninus of Grado received the pallium from him.

Hildebrand, later Gregory VII, was born in Tuscany between 1020 and 1025 and died at Salerno on 25 May 1085. His name meant a bright flame to friends and a brand of hell to foes. His father Bonizo was called a carpenter by some and a peasant by others, and his mother's name is unrecorded. Schooled at Santa Maria on the Aventine under his uncle Abbot Laurentius, he absorbed Cluny's austere reform spirit and became a Benedictine monk at Rome.

He served John Gratian, becoming his chaplain when Gratian became Gregory VI. As pope he pressed the rule that no one should receive a church benefice without papal sanction. In 1074 he planned an eastern expedition to free Christians from the Seljuk Turks and to reunite East and West, sending Venice's patriarch to Constantinople. At the 1075 Lenten Synod he excommunicated Robert Guiscard for invading Capua and Benevento.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-pope-st-leo-i:
Leo III was a Roman, son of Atyuppius and Elizabeth. He was elected the very day his predecessor was buried, 26 December 795, and consecrated the next day, perhaps to forestall Frankish meddling. At election he held St Susanna's cardinal-priesthood and seemingly led the pontifical treasury. He sent Charlemagne the keys of St Peter's confession and the city's standard.

Charlemagne answered with congratulations and a share of Avar treasure, wealth that made Leo a great benefactor of Rome's churches and charities. On 25 April 799, kinsmen of Adrian I attacked him in the Greater Litanies procession, dashing him down and trying to tear out his tongue and eyes. Left bleeding, he was carried by night to St Erasmus monastery on the Coelian Hill. He worked closely with Charlemagne thereafter: Salzburg became Bavaria's metropolitan city, Northumbria's Eardulf regained his kingdom, and Leo settled disputes between York and Canterbury. He died in 816.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-pope-st-sixtu:
Sixtus II was elected on 31 August 257 and martyred at Rome on 6 August 258. His origin is unknown. The Liber Pontificalis calls him Greek by birth, but that likely confuses him with the Greek philosopher sharing his name, author of the Sentences of Xystus. Under his predecessor Stephen, Rome had quarrelled sharply with Africa and Asia over rebaptizing heretics. Sixtus, called a good and peaceful priest, was more conciliatory and restored friendly relations.

Valerian's first edict had forced Christians into pagan cult and banned cemetery assemblies on pain of exile or death. Sixtus somehow carried out his pastoral work unmolested. In early August 258 a crueller edict followed. He was led away, and the likelier account says he was brought back to the cemetery for execution. Damasus's inscription on his Callistus tomb can be read either way. The entry also recalls his meeting with Lawrence as he was led to death.

Sixtus III was consecrated on 31 July 432 and died in 440. Before his accession he stood prominent among Rome's clergy and corresponded with Augustine. He reigned through the Nestorian and Pelagian controversies. His conciliatory temper probably drew false charges of leaning toward those heresies.

As pope he approved Ephesus's acts and laboured to reconcile Cyril of Alexandria with John of Antioch. In the Pelagian fight he blocked Julian of Eclanum's return to communion. He upheld Rome's supremacy over Illyricum against local bishops and Constantinople's Proclus. At Rome he restored the Liberian Basilica, enlarged St Lawrence-Without-the-Walls, and Valentinian III gave precious gifts for St Peter's and the Lateran. A work claiming Bassus charged him with crime counts as a forgery. He wrote eight letters, but not the works on riches, false teachers, and chastity ascribed to him.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-pope-stephen-: Stephen, a priest unanimously elected about 23 March 752 on Zachary's death, was struck with apoplexy on the third day after election while attending to domestic affairs, and died the next day. Because he died before consecration, earlier writers left him off the pope list. By the Roman church's long-standing practice he is now generally counted among the popes, a split practice that has tangled the numbering of the Stephens ever since.

Stephen, later counted as Stephen II or III, won unanimous election in St Mary Major's, with consecration on 26 March or 3 April 752. He died on 26 April 757. At once he faced Lombards bent on ruling all Italy. They had taken Ravenna in 751, ending the Byzantine exarchs, and now aimed at Rome's duchy. Appeals to Constantinople failed.

Stephen turned to prayer and to Pepin and the Franks. As a last resort he went to Gaul and pleaded before the Frankish king. Pepin received him warmly, was crowned by him as King of the Franks, and promised at Kiersey to defend him and restore the exarchate to St Peter. Pepin forced the Alps in 754 and made Aistulf swear to return Ravenna and other cities. When Aistulf broke faith and besieged Rome in January 756, Pepin crossed again and forced submission. Stephen then received the exarchate and Pentapolis.

Stephen reigned from 896 to 897 and died about August 897. A Roman, son of the priest John, Formosus had made him bishop of Anagni, possibly against his will. He became pope about May 896. Whether from evil passion or, more likely, compulsion by Emperor Lambert and his mother Ageltruda, he had Formosus's body exhumed.

In January 897 the corpse stood before an unwilling synod of Roman clergy, with a deacon answering for the dead pope. Formosus was condemned for acting as bishop after deposition and for moving from Porto to Rome. The body was stripped of vestments, lost two fingers of its right hand, was dressed as a layman, and was thrown into the Tiber. Stephen forced Formosus's ordinands to resign and granted a few church privileges before he was strangled to death.

Stephen's reign ran from 929 to 931, ending with his February or March 931 death. He took the papal office at the end of 928 or the start of 929. A Roman, son of Teudemund, he had been cardinal-priest of St Anastasia. As pope he granted monastery privileges in France and Italy, and St Peter's holds his grave. Nothing more is known of him.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-pope-sylveste:
Gerbert, later Sylvester II, reigned from 999 to 1003. Born near Aurillac in Auvergne about 940 to 950 to humble parents, he died at Rome on 12 May 1003. Trained at Aurillac's monastery, he was taken to Spain, studying at Barcelona and under Arab teachers at Cordova and Seville. At Rome, John XIII commended him to Otto I, who sent him to teach at Reims.

Otto II gave him the poor abbey of Bobbio in 983, and Gerbert returned to Reims teaching and helping raise Hugh Capet to the throne. After Adalbero died in 988, Arnulph took Reims, but a synod deposed him for alleged treason in 991 and Gerbert succeeded him. Later he became Otto III's teacher, went with him to Italy, and in 998 Gregory V made him archbishop of Ravenna. On Gregory's death in February 999, Gerbert was elected through the emperor's influence and took the name Sylvester, the first French pope. He attacked simony and concubinage.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-pope-theodore:
Theodore II, son of Photius, held the papacy only twenty days. Neither his birth date nor his accession date is known, but he was probably pope during December 897. In synod he restored clerics degraded by Stephen VI-VII and ordered the forced resignation acts they had signed to be burned. He formally recognized the validity of orders conferred by Formosus.

He had Formosus's body, thrown into the Tiber and washed ashore by a flood, reburied in St Peter's. Frodoard, his contemporary, says clergy loved him, and he loved and promoted peace. Frodoard also calls him temperate, chaste, and charitable to the poor.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-pope-urban-ii:
Uberto Crivelli, later Urban III, reigned from 1185 to 1187. Milan-born to the noble Crivelli, Lucius III made him cardinal in 1182, and Milan's archbishop in 1185. When Lucius died at Verona on 25 November, Uberto was elected the same day and crowned on 1 December. He inherited his predecessor's feud with Frederick Barbarossa, sharpened by old personal enmity from Milan's sack in 1162.

Constance, Sicily's heiress, married Frederick's son Henry at Milan in January 1186. That marriage wrecked the popes' laborious work of checking emperors in Italy and guarding the Papal States, and lost the papacy its Norman support. Frederick seized vacant German sees' revenues and suppressed nunneries for their property. Frederick closed the Alpine passes to papal messengers, and Henry ravaged the Papal States at his bidding. At Gelnhausen in 1187 Frederick won Germany's bishops to his side. Urban summoned Frederick to Verona, but the Veronese blocked any excommunication.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-pope-urban-vi:
Giambattista Castagna was born at Rome on 4 August 1521 and died there on 27 September 1590, twelve days after his election on 15 September. His father was a Genoese nobleman and his mother a Roman, sister of Cardinal Jacovazzi. He took doctorates in civil and canon law at Bologna. He served his uncle Cardinal Verallo as auditor and datary on a French legation. Julius III made him referendary and, in March 1553, archbishop of Rossano.

He governed Fano and Perugia, settled a long Terni-Spoleto boundary quarrel under Pius IV, and showed prudence and learning at Trent from 1562 to 1563. He spent seven years as nuncio in Spain, resigned Rossano in 1573, served as nuncio to Venice, governor of Bologna, and legate extraordinary at Cologne.

Maffeo Barberini was born at Florence in April 1568 and died at Rome on 29 July 1644. His father died when he was three, and his mother brought him to Rome. Jesuits schooled him at the Collegio Romano, and he graduated in law from Pisa in 1589. Clement VIII named him Fano's governor and prothonotary, and in 1601 he carried felicitations to Henry IV on the dauphin's birth.

In 1604 he became archbishop of Nazareth and nuncio to Paris. Paul V made him cardinal in 1606. As legate of Bologna from 1617 he prepared for higher office. Fifty-five cardinals entered conclave in July 1623, and on 6 August Barberini won fifty votes as Urban VIII. His reign became famous for Barberini nepotism: nephews gained cardinalates, commands, and principalities, and immense riches flowed to the family. Twice he had theologians test whether nephews might keep their gains, and twice they ruled yes.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-pope-victor-i:
Gebhard, later Victor II, was born about 1018 and died at Arezzo on 28 July 1057. His birthplace is disputed between Bavaria and Swabia. Count Hartwig and Countess Baliza were his parents. Henry III counted him a kinsman, and his uncle, Bishop Gebhard of Ratisbon, presented him at Goslar at Christmas 1042 for Eichstätt. Henry made him bishop of Eichstätt.

Gebhard proved a good bishop and prudent statesman. He attended Henry's Rome crowning and Leo IX's Mainz synod. By then he was Henry's most influential councillor. On his advice Henry recalled a German army marching to aid Leo IX against the Normans, advice he reportedly regretted as pope. In 1053 he took Bavaria's regency for three-year-old Henry IV, defending imperial rights. As pope he fought simony and clerical concubinage, holding a great Florence synod on Pentecost 1055 with the emperor and 120 bishops, confirming decrees and deposing offenders.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-raymond-vii:
Raymond the Seventh, Count of Toulouse and son of Raymond the Sixth, was born at Beaucaire in 1197 and died at Milhaud in 1249. This encyclopedia entry tells that he married a sister of the King of Aragon and helped his father win back the family estates. In January 1224 Amaury de Montfort, reduced to the lordship of Narbonne, made a treaty with him, but ceded his southern rights to Louis the Eighth of France.

In vain Raymond offered his obedience to the assembly of Bourges in 1226, and a new Crusade was decreed. Louis seized Avignon and occupied Languedoc without resistance, but died on his way north on 8 November 1226 at Montpensier. Raymond then profited from Blanche of Castile's weakness, taking places from Imbert de Beaujeu, the French king's seneschal. That success lasted briefly: fresh crusader bands plundered the Toulouse country in 1228, and Raymond soon lost nearly all his strongholds.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-referendarii:
Referendarii, from refero, to inform, held a papal office with roots at the Byzantine Court. This encyclopedia entry explains that there, officials reported to the emperor on petitioners' memorials and carried the emperor's orders on those memorials to the judges. In Merovingian Frankish times, the later chancellor bore the title referendarius. In the Papal Curia the office of referendarii Apostolici arose in the Middle Ages.

They took in all petitions sent to the Holy See, reported on them to the pope, and offered him advice. Treatment varied with the question: a favour might be granted or refused, while a dispute went to a judge if the pope so decided. The referendarii handled all arrangements for these papal decisions, and the entry notes that Pius the Tenth later reshaped the Curia's offices. Bangen, Thomassinus and a German history of the modern Catholic Church supply its sources.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-regionarii:
Regionarii were the clerics and officials of the Church of Rome who belonged neither to the papal palace nor to Rome's titular churches. Instead, each had one of the city's regions, or wards, as his official district. Augustus had divided Rome into fourteen regions for civil administration, and from the fourth century a church division into seven regions grew up beside it, gradually replacing the civil lines.

Many branches of church administration followed the seven regions. Care of the poor, upkeep of the churches, and other work belonging first of all to the deacons fell under them, one deacon standing over each region. The entry traces how this regional system shaped the early medieval government of the Roman Church, and it cites De Rossi, Phillips, and Hinschius as its sources.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-sandwich-isla:
The Sandwich Islands, now Hawaii, form a vicariate apostolic covering the whole Hawaiian group. They lie just inside the northern tropic, between 18 and 22 degrees north and 154 and 160 degrees west of Greenwich. Eight islands are inhabited: Kauai, Niihau, Oahu, Molokai, Lanai, Maui, Kahoolawe, and Hawaii, with 191,909 people in 1910. Its entry in the 1913 Catholic Encyclopedia traces Catholic beginnings in the Pacific.

The first Catholic priests reached Honolulu on 9 July 1827: Alexis Bachelot, prefect apostolic, Abraham Armand, both Frenchmen, and Patrick Short, an Irishman. All belonged to the Congregation of the Sacred Hearts, called Picpus from its Paris street. Sent by Leo XII, they found New England Protestant missionaries already at work since 1820, and the entry follows the rivalry and growth that followed.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-st-anselm-duk:
St. Anselm, duke of Forum Julii, the modern Friuli in north-eastern Italy, left the world to serve God in a monastery, and this entry follows a nobleman turned founder. In 750 he built a monastery at Fanano, on land given him by Aistulph, King of the Lombards, who had married Anselm's sister Gisaltruda. And two years later he raised Nonantula, a short distance north-east of Modena.

Going to Rome, he received the Benedictine habit from Stephen III, who made him abbot of Nonantula. And, charitable and able, he founded many hospices where monks sheltered and cared for the poor and feeble Desiderius, Aistulph's successor, banished him for seven years to Monte Cassino. But after Charlemagne captured Desiderius he returned, dying at Nonantula in 803 after fifty years as abbot.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-st-ferdinand-:
Ferdinand III, king of Leon and Castile until 1252, joined reconquest with a reputation for justice and restraint. Born near Salamanca in 1198 to Alfonso IX of Leon and Berengeria of Castile, he took Castile in 1217. His mother renounced that crown in his favour. Leon followed in 1230, amid strife over uniting the crowns. The Catholic Encyclopedia piece of 1913 dates his death at Seville to 30 May 1252.

He chose wise counsellors, administered justice strictly, and refused to overburden subjects with tax, fearing one poor woman's curse more than a Saracen army. Married in 1219 to Beatrice of Swabia, he fathered seven children. His highest aims were spreading the faith and good rule, and he joined the Third Order of St. Francis. The entry presents a conqueror king remembered as a just and pious ruler.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-st-henry-ii:
Henry II, German king and Holy Roman Emperor until 1024, ruled with sober sense, energy, and conscience. Son of Henry the Quarrelsome and Gisela of Burgundy, born in 972, he was destined in youth for the priesthood and learned church affairs early. He strengthened Germany's church while treating its institutions as pivots of power, in Otto the Great's manner. The Catholic Encyclopedia article of 1913 dates his death at Grona, near Göttingen, to 13 July 1024.

With learning and piety he joined practical common sense, attempting only the possible and settling troubles by amiable, reasonable methods. Sick and fevered, he still traversed the empire to keep the peace, using power always to adjust disputes. The entry presents an emperor who went his way circumspectly, never flamboyant, always conscientious: a ruler whose prudence was itself a form of strength.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-st-paulinus-i:
Paulinus II, patriarch of Aquileia, served Charlemagne as scholar, courtier, and churchman. Born at Premariacco near Cividale about 730 to 740, he was raised in the patriarchal schools and mastered Latin letters, law, Scripture, and patristic learning. Charlemagne called him to France in 776 as royal master of grammar.

There he met Alcuin, Peter of Pisa, and the leading minds of the age, and helped restore learning in the West. Charles rewarded him with lands and named him patriarch of Aquileia in 787. He handled delicate relations with Istria and Grado, and wrote poems and treatises. He died in 802, a model of the scholar bishop of the Carolingian renewal.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-suppression-o:
Henry VIII's destruction of the English monasteries ranks among the great events of the sixteenth century, and this entry retells it as a planned political act. Monks, called the great standing army of Rome, formed a bulwark of the papal system. After the king's breach with Rome, royal supervision of visitations soon followed, with Thomas Cromwell as vicar-general in spirituals in 1534.

Commissions of visitation followed in January 1535, but the entry stresses that suppression was already royal policy before any visitation reported. Parliament in 1536 was asked to hand over the smaller houses, both to refill an empty treasury and to forestall religious opposition. Later pages track the dissolutions house by house and account for the wealth, from palaces and war spending to pensions for displaced religious.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-valentinian-i:
Valentinian II, Flavius Valentinianus, reigned from 375 to 392. Born in Gaul about 371, he was murdered at Vienne in Dauphiny on 15 May 392. His father was Valentinian I and his mother Justina, the emperor's second wife, yet he ruled in name far more than in fact. While Gratian ruled in the East, Magnus Maximus held most of the West, leaving Italy alone to Valentinian, and even there his mother Justina, with whom he lived at Milan, truly ruled.

Maximus invaded Italy in 387, four years after seizing the northern provinces, and Justina fled with Valentinian to Thessalonica, seeking help from Theodosius in the East. Maximus fell, but Justina soon died, and Valentinian fell under the evil sway of Arbogast, who had him assassinated later. Weak but just and peace-loving, he stands as a puppet emperor in a crumbling West.

Valentinian III reigned from 425 to 455, born at Ravenna on 3 July 419, died at Rome on 16 March 455. Son of Constantius III and Galla Placidia, daughter of Theodosius, he succeeded Honorius. In 437 he wed his cousin Eudoxia at Constantinople. His years on the throne saw the western empire crumble province by province. Roman control of Britain lapsed in 446, while Aëtius could not keep Gaul clear of Franks, Burgundians, and Huns; Africa had already slipped away in 439, when the Vandals beat Boniface.

In 425 all schismatics were ordered to leave Rome, and in the same year the clergy's immunity from civil courts was reaffirmed, though Valentinian later withdrew that privilege in 452. The entry follows his reign through the empire's slide to his assassination in 455, giving a compact life of an emperor who reigned long and ruled little.
doe-osti-3012130-pulsed-magnet-power-sys: NSLS-II got pulsed magnets, and this DOE text covers the power systems. The pages detail the findings. The accelerator folks get their data. The magnets were pulsed. The data were accelerator. The facility was NSLS-II. The systems were power.
egyptian-tales-translated-from-the-papyr:
W. M. Flinders Petrie's Egyptian Tales, Second Series, translates stories of the Eighteenth to Nineteenth Dynasties. Petrie warns that these are not fairy tales in the usual sense, since they relate the doings of men and women who are human, at times all too human.

Supernatural elements, he explains, belong to the beliefs and motives of the people pictured, and most of what happens might occur today where ancient beliefs still hold. No being in the volume could properly be called a fairy. Tristram Ellis illustrates the tales. Readers who enjoyed the first series will find this second volume equally vivid and human.
expositions-of-holy-scripture-st-matthew:
Alexander Maclaren's Expositions of Holy Scripture: St. Matthew, Chapters Nine to Twenty-Eight, continues his sermon expositions of the Gospels. Maclaren treats each passage as a text for preaching, drawing out its devotional and moral meaning.

Expositions include Christ's Encouragements, Soul-Healing First, The Call of Matthew, The Touch of Faith, The Obscure Apostles, and Christ's Charge to His Heralds. Later pieces treat John's doubts, the friend of publicans and sinners, the rest giver, and the Pharisees' Sabbath. Readers who value Maclaren's preaching will find this volume, like its companions, clear, warm and richly applied.
freytag-pictures-of-german-life-xviiixix:
The concluding volume of Freytag's Pictures of German Life, in English, finishes the story of Germany in the 1700s and 1800s. From Enlightenment salons to the brink of national unification, the narrative follows one long making of modern life. Workshops, schools, and parliaments all change across its pages.

Freytag keeps his novelist's eye on character while commanding a historian's range of fact. Middle-class families rise; old orders adapt or vanish; cities swallow villages. The volume completes a four-part panorama that taught generations of Germans their own everyday past. Its sympathy for ordinary people stays its chief virtue. English readers receive the whole arc of the project in this and the companion volumes.
freytag-pictures-of-german-life-xvxvii-c:
Volume Two of Freytag's Pictures of German Life, in English, completes his panorama of the fifteenth through seventeenth centuries. Trade routes, craft guilds, and family customs share pages with the wars of religion. Luther's age and its long aftermath receive the closest attention in this concluding half.

Freytag follows households through plague, inflation, and invasion with a storyteller's patience. The detail is a treasure house: how people dressed, worshipped, bargained, and buried their dead. A novelist's gifts keep the material breathing rather than dusty. Together the two volumes taught German readers to see their own past in daily things. English readers gain the same education in translation.
govdocs-nsarchive-Briefing_Book_climate-:
Rachel Santarsiero edited this briefing book, number 905, published on September 30, 2025. It is the second part of a series on climate information vanishing from United States government sources. Its subject is a White House effort to remove and change data about climate change.

Outside organizations, the posting reports, were working to rescue climate data before it disappeared for good. The record connects that removal effort to distorted science and to deregulation. It documents a fight over public information itself: who controls the numbers that climate policy depends on, and what happens when they are taken down.
king-edward-iii:
King Edward the Third is a history play from Shakespeare's age, credited in part to William Shakespeare. Its cast pairs the English court with the French. Edward the Third heads the list, with his son, the Prince of Wales. The earls of Warwick, Derby, and Salisbury stand among his lords.

Across the channel stand King John of France and his sons Charles and Philip. Queen Philippa and the Countess of Salisbury hold the women's parts.
